name: Barbell Curl
rom_notes: Full ROM: let the bar descend to full elbow extension for a deep stretch, curl close to the top. Source warns curls are among the most ROM-abused lifts — go all the way down.
regional_bias: overall biceps (fixed supinated grip; both heads loaded through big-load full ROM)
cues: Pin elbows at sides, supinate fully, control the eccentric to a dead-bottom stretch. Heavy-range anchor — respond well to straight sets; one of the more systemically fatiguing curls.

name: EZ-Bar Curl
rom_notes: Full ROM with the semi-supinated cambered grip reducing wrist strain versus the straight bar; descend to a full stretch.
regional_bias: overall biceps with slightly less supination than the straight bar (more wrist-friendly)
cues: Use the angled grooves to spare the wrists; same full-ROM, elbows-pinned rules as the barbell curl. A systemically fatiguing basic suited to heavier ranges.

name: Dumbbell Curl
rom_notes: Full ROM with free supination available; descend to a deep stretch at the bottom. Each arm works independently.
regional_bias: overall biceps; supination twist option emphasizes the supination function
cues: Load hangs from the closed hand (crush-grip). Supinate as you curl to load the biceps' supination role; full eccentric to the stretch each rep.

name: Dumbbell Twist (Supination) Curl
rom_notes: Begin neutral/pronated at the bottom and actively supinate through the curl to maximally load the supination function; full stretch at bottom.
regional_bias: biceps supination emphasis (source's named example of loading the supination function)
cues: Explicitly the 'load the supination function' category from the source. Start hand neutral, finish fully supinated with pinky high; DB hangs from the closed hand.

name: Incline Dumbbell Curl
rom_notes: Reclined torso puts the shoulder in extension, placing the long head under deep stretch at the bottom. Named example of the source's 'load the stretch' category.
regional_bias: long head of biceps (stretch-position emphasis)
cues: Let arms hang back behind the torso for maximum long-head stretch; don't shorten the bottom ROM. Source's go-to stretch-position curl. DB hangs from the hand.

name: Preacher Curl
rom_notes: Pad fixes the upper arm in shoulder flexion; heavy load lands at the stretched bottom position. Lower to a full stretch — don't bounce out of the bottom.
regional_bias: short head of biceps; heavy stretched-position loading
cues: Triceps against the pad, control the eccentric to a deep stretch; the bottom is the hardest point so don't cut it short.

name: Machine Preacher Curl
rom_notes: Pad supports the upper arm; machine cam keeps tension through the range including the stretched bottom. Used in the source's sample mesocycles.
regional_bias: short head of biceps; low-skill stable loading good for myoreps/drop sets
cues: Handles are supported so grip is not limiting — ideal for myoreps and drop sets where re-loading is cheap. Full stretch at the bottom.

name: Spider Curl
rom_notes: Chest braced on an incline, arms hang vertically so peak tension is at the fully shortened (contracted) top — the source's named peak-contraction example.
regional_bias: peak contraction / short head emphasis
cues: High mind-muscle-connection move — source notes it may not be ideal at very low (5-10) or very high (20-30) reps for MMC reasons; squeeze hard at the top. Almost no synergists, so rest can be very short.

name: Concentration Curl
rom_notes: Seated, elbow braced against inner thigh; arm isolated for a strong peak contraction and full ROM. One arm at a time.
regional_bias: short head / peak contraction; strong supination cue
cues: Brace the elbow on the thigh, supinate hard and squeeze the top. High MMC, low systemic cost; DB hangs from the closed hand.

name: Cable Curl
rom_notes: Constant cable tension through the full range, including the bottom stretch and the top. Used in source's light (20-30) sample sessions.
regional_bias: overall biceps; constant-tension loading ideal for high-rep and drop sets
cues: Cable keeps tension on at lockout; source calls cables nearly ideal for biceps drop sets. Keep elbows pinned, full ROM.

name: Machine Curl (One-Arm)
rom_notes: Fixed path with the cam providing resistance through the range; the source cites a 'machine one-arm curl' as a usable weekly variation.
regional_bias: overall biceps; supported, low-skill, easy to re-load for myoreps/occlusion
cues: Supported handle means grip and forearms are not limiting — good for myoreps and occlusion where forearm endurance otherwise caps you.

name: Hammer Curl
rom_notes: Neutral (thumbs-up) grip held throughout; full ROM down to a stretch. Neutral grip shifts emphasis to brachialis and brachioradialis.
regional_bias: brachialis and brachioradialis (neutral grip removes the supination demand)
cues: Keep the wrist neutral throughout; lets you handle heavier load than supinated curls. DB hangs from the closed hand.

name: Reverse Curl
rom_notes: Pronated (palms-down) grip; full ROM down to a stretch. Pronation puts the biceps at a mechanical disadvantage so brachioradialis and brachialis dominate.
regional_bias: brachioradialis / forearm and brachialis (pronated grip)
cues: Palms down, keep wrists stable; loads the brachioradialis and wrist extensors hardest. Expect to use lighter loads than supinated curls.

name: Triceps Pushdown
rom_notes: Elbows pinned at the sides; lock out at the bottom, allow a full stretch at the top. Source calls pushdowns ideal at 20-30 reps with minimal synergist involvement.
regional_bias: lateral and medial heads (arm at the side keeps the long head shortened)
cues: Lowest-systemic-demand triceps move — source's go-to for myoreps, drop sets, and high reps. Pin elbows, full lockout, controlled return to stretch.

name: Rope Triceps Pushdown
rom_notes: Rope allows the hands to spread and pronate apart at lockout for a stronger peak contraction; elbows stay pinned, full stretch at top.
regional_bias: lateral and medial heads; rope spread adds end-range contraction
cues: Spread the rope ends apart at the bottom and turn pinkies out for a hard lockout. Low fatigue, great for drop sets and myoreps.

name: Overhead Cable Rope Triceps Extension
rom_notes: Arms overhead put the shoulder in flexion, stretching the long head deeply at the bottom. Source explicitly lists the cable/rope overhead extension and stresses deep stretch.
regional_bias: long head of triceps (overhead = long-head stretch bias)
cues: Constant cable tension with a deep overhead stretch — triceps 'love the stretch.' Long-head emphasis the source notes may overlap with what back training already provides.

name: Overhead Dumbbell Triceps Extension
rom_notes: Shoulder fully flexed overhead; lower the DB behind the head to a deep long-head stretch. Free weight loads the closed hand overhead.
regional_bias: long head of triceps (overhead stretch)
cues: Keep elbows pointed forward, lower deep behind the head for the long-head stretch. The DB hangs from / is squeezed by the closed hand overhead (crush-grip).

name: Overhead Barbell / EZ-Bar Triceps Extension
rom_notes: Bar lowered behind the head with shoulders flexed for a deep long-head stretch. Source lists barbell, EZ, seated barbell and seated EZ overhead extensions explicitly.
regional_bias: long head of triceps (overhead stretch); heavier than the DB/cable versions
cues: Source notes forearm fatigue limits this in the 20-30 range — best in 10-20. Lower behind the head for the stretch; EZ bar spares the wrists.

name: Skullcrusher (Lying Triceps Extension)
rom_notes: Lying; lower the bar to the forehead or behind the head for a deep stretch. Source flags elbow injury risk if rushed — use controlled eccentrics and pauses.
regional_bias: long and medial heads; partial long-head stretch (more if lowered behind the head)
cues: One of the named isolation choices. Slow the eccentric and pause — source warns elbow/shoulder injury is possible if rushed. Lower behind the head for more long-head stretch.

name: JM Press
rom_notes: Hybrid between a close-grip press and a skullcrusher — bar tracks toward the upper chest/chin with elbows forward. Source calls it safely compatible with the heavy 5-10 range.
regional_bias: overall triceps (medial/lateral emphasis); heaviest of the triceps moves
cues: Source's heavy anchor — best in the 5-10 range, an early-block high-stress staple. Keep elbows forward and let the bar settle near the chin before pressing.

name: Close-Grip Bench Press
rom_notes: Shoulder-width grip; elbows tucked, bar to the lower chest. Source uses incline close-grip presses as the compound finisher in overhead-extension pre-exhaust supersets.
regional_bias: overall triceps (medial/lateral) with pec/front-delt assistance
cues: Tuck elbows and keep the grip ~shoulder width — too narrow stresses the wrists. A heavy compound triceps anchor; pairs well as the back half of a pre-exhaust superset.

name: Triceps Dip
rom_notes: Upright torso biases the triceps; descend to a deep stretch then lock out. Source notes instability makes dips better in 10-20 than 20-30, and slow eccentrics reveal which elbow angle taxes triceps most.
regional_bias: overall triceps (lateral/medial emphasis with upright torso)
cues: Source's flagship compound triceps move and pre-exhaust target. Stay upright for triceps bias, control the eccentric (injury risk if rushed); follow weighted dips with unweighted down-sets for huge MMC.

name: Conventional Barbell Deadlift
rom_notes: Bar from floor to standing lockout; hips travel through full flexion-to-extension. Knees flex more than in RDL/stiff-leg so quads contribute off the floor. Reset each rep for a true dead start; touch-and-go shortens the bottom.
regional_bias: whole posterior chain; relatively erector- and quad-dominant vs RDL/stiff-leg, with semitendinosus > biceps femoris within the hamstrings
cues: Pull slack into the bar before lifting; brace hard, keep spine rigid and neutral, drive the floor away. Hips and shoulders rise together. Grip the bar as hard as possible (irradiation). Use mixed/hook grip or straps once pulling strength outruns grip.

name: Sumo Deadlift
rom_notes: Wide stance, hands inside knees, more upright torso and lower hips than conventional. Shorter bar path; higher knee-extension demand and more adductor/quad involvement, lower spinal-flexor moment than conventional.
regional_bias: more quad/adductor and less lower-back demand than conventional; strong glute and adductor-magnus contribution
cues: Shins vertical from the front, knees tracking over toes. 'Rip the floor apart' between the feet to load the hips and engage the quads. Open the hips, stay over mid-foot, drive knees out through lockout.

name: Trap-Bar (Hex-Bar) Deadlift
rom_notes: Neutral-grip handles centre the load through the body; more knee flexion and a more upright torso than conventional. Floor-to-lockout ROM. Reduced erector-spinae demand makes it a good deadlift variant for lifters with lower-back issues.
regional_bias: more quad-dominant and lower erector-spinae stress than straight-bar deadlift; load line through the body reduces shear
cues: Stand in the centre of the bar, neutral grip. Brace, sit the hips slightly lower than conventional, push the floor away. Keeps the load close so the back works less and the legs more.

name: Deficit Deadlift
rom_notes: Lifter stands on a 1-4 inch plate/platform, increasing range of motion and bottom-position stretch on the glutes and hamstrings. Used for glute emphasis (deficit sumo) and off-the-floor strength.
regional_bias: greater bottom-range stretch on glutes and hamstrings than floor pulls; deficit sumo is a favoured heavy compound for glute growth
cues: Keep a neutral spine despite the deeper start; only use as much deficit as you can reach without rounding. Feel the stretch in the hips and hamstrings at the bottom.

name: Romanian Deadlift (RDL)
rom_notes: Knees held slightly flexed at a near-constant angle; movement is hip flexion/extension. Bar lowered until a deep hamstring stretch (usually mid-shin, not the floor) then driven back to lockout. Isometric-knee hinge — quads only stabilize.
regional_bias: hamstring-dominant hip hinge; targets semitendinosus more than the stiff-leg deadlift does
tempo: 2-3s eccentric, pause or slow reversal at the stretch — never bounce
cues: Soft-but-fixed knees, push the hips straight back, keep the bar against the legs. Lower until you feel a strong (not painful-overbearing) hamstring stretch, then come all the way up to reset. Control every rep; rapid reversals at the stretch are dangerous for the hamstrings.

name: Step (Deficit) Romanian Deadlift
rom_notes: RDL performed standing on a ~15 cm step so the bar can travel below foot level, increasing trunk flexion and posterior-chain elongation. EMG shows higher gluteus maximus, semitendinosus and erector-spinae (longissimus) excitation than RDL or stiff-leg via the larger stretch.
regional_bias: highest overall posterior-chain excitation of the RDL family due to greater ROM/stretch; emphasizes semitendinosus and gluteus maximus
tempo: slow eccentric, pause at the deep stretch
cues: Same hinge as the RDL but on a platform — let the bar pass below the toes for a deeper stretch. Only go as deep as you keep a neutral spine. The extra elongation is the whole point; don't rush the bottom.

name: Stiff-Leg Deadlift (SLDL)
rom_notes: Knees held essentially extended throughout; bar travels from floor to lockout via pure hip hinge, giving the widest ROM of the hinge family. Strong hamstring and glute stretch; greater gluteus-maximus excitation than RDL but slightly less semitendinosus.
regional_bias: glute-max-biased hip hinge (more than RDL); within hamstrings, semitendinosus still > biceps femoris but less ST emphasis than RDL
tempo: 2-3s eccentric, pause/slow reversal at the stretch
cues: Near-straight legs, hinge from the hips, keep the bar close. Lower to a deep hamstring stretch and come all the way up to reset each rep. Keep hip-hinge work to 5-10 reps so the lower-back erectors don't fail before the hamstrings.

name: Dumbbell Romanian Deadlift
rom_notes: Same hip-hinge as the barbell RDL but dumbbells held at the sides allow a slightly deeper, less bar-restricted descent and let the load pass beside the legs. Hamstring-dominant with knees near-fixed.
regional_bias: hamstring-dominant hip hinge; dumbbells permit a marginally larger stretch ROM than the barbell
cues: Hips back, soft knees, dumbbells tracking down the front of the legs. Let the DBs sink past the knees for a deeper stretch than a barbell allows, then drive the hips through to lockout.

name: Single-Leg Romanian Deadlift
rom_notes: Hinge over one stance leg while the rear leg counterbalances; large unilateral hip-flexion ROM with a strong single-hamstring stretch. Adds frontal-plane stability demand. Unilateral stiff-leg variants show even more pronounced semitendinosus emphasis.
regional_bias: single-leg hamstring/glute hinge with extra gluteus-medius and anti-rotation demand; strong semitendinosus emphasis
tempo: controlled eccentric, pause at the stretch
cues: Hinge over the stance hip, let the back leg rise as a counterweight, keep the hips square (resist rotation). Reach the load toward the floor for a deep stretch, then return to a tall finish. Use a wall or rack to balance if needed.

name: Barbell Good Morning
rom_notes: Bar on the upper back; hip-hinge with near-fixed knees lowers the torso toward parallel and back up. Loads the hamstrings and erectors heavily through the trunk lever. EMG: similar pattern to RDL but more semitendinosus and less biceps femoris.
regional_bias: hamstring + spinal-erector hinge; more semitendinosus and less biceps femoris than the RDL, with heavy lower-back demand
cues: Bar racked on the traps, soft knees, hinge the hips straight back and let the chest fall toward parallel while keeping a rigid neutral spine. Good substitute for the RDL when you'd rather load the back than lift from the floor. Stay conservative on load — the long lever is demanding on the erectors.

name: 45-Degree Back Extension (Hip Extension)
rom_notes: Pads at the upper thighs; trunk hinges over the hip from full flexion (torso hanging) to neutral. Hip-extension hinge against gravity perpendicular to the torso. Bourne et al. found 45-degree hip extension elicits very high biceps femoris and semitendinosus activation — greater than the stiff-leg deadlift.
regional_bias: rounded-back/glute-focused or flat-back/hamstring-focused depending on spinal cue; very high hamstring (biceps femoris + semitendinosus) activation
tempo: controlled both directions, squeeze at the top
cues: Pad just below the hip crease so the hips can hinge freely. Round the upper back and curl up for glute bias, or keep a flat back and hinge purely at the hips for hamstring bias. Hold a plate or band for added load. Don't hyperextend past neutral.

name: Glute-Ham Raise (GHR)
rom_notes: On a GHD/GHR bench: combines hip extension at the bottom with knee flexion to raise the torso, so the hamstrings work at both joints. Heavily loads the hamstrings through knee flexion against bodyweight; can add a plate.
regional_bias: whole hamstring complex worked at hip and knee simultaneously; strong knee-flexion stimulus with a hip-extension component
cues: Anchor the feet, keep the hips extended and torso rigid, pull yourself up by flexing the knees and driving the toes into the platform. Lower under control. Add a plate held to the chest or a band once bodyweight is easy.

name: Nordic Hamstring Curl
rom_notes: Knees anchored, hips held extended; the lifter lowers the rigid torso to the floor purely by eccentric knee flexion, then pulls back. Maximal eccentric knee-flexion overload — one of the highest hamstring (biceps femoris + semitendinosus) activators, greater than the stiff-leg deadlift.
regional_bias: eccentric-dominant knee-flexion overload of the whole hamstring; strong biceps femoris and semitendinosus recruitment
tempo: slow controlled eccentric; assist back up with hands/band
cues: Anchor the ankles, keep a straight line from knees to head (hips fully extended, don't pike). Lower as slowly as possible, catch with the hands, then pull back up using the hamstrings. Use a band or push off the floor to assist the concentric until strong enough.

name: Lying (Prone) Leg Curl
rom_notes: Prone on the pad; knee flexion brings the heel to the glutes against a roller pad. Hips extended, so the hamstrings work from a moderately lengthened (hip) but knee-isolated position. Higher biceps-femoris activation than the stiff-leg deadlift.
regional_bias: knee-flexion isolation biased toward the biceps femoris (both upper and lower portions); prone hip angle differs from seated
tempo: controlled, full ROM, pad to glutes each rep
cues: Start from a fully extended knee and curl the pad all the way to the butt every rep — partial reps don't count unless training lengthened partials. Keep the hips pinned to the pad; don't let them pop up. Control the eccentric.

name: Seated Leg Curl
rom_notes: Seated with the hips flexed (~90 deg), so the hamstrings start lengthened at the hip while the knee flexes against the pad. The flexed-hip position trains the hamstrings at a longer length and is a strong stretch-mediated stimulus; elicits high hamstring activation, more than the stiff-leg deadlift.
regional_bias: knee-flexion isolation under hip flexion (lengthened hamstring); favoured for stretch-mediated growth and high-rep work
tempo: controlled, full ROM, emphasize the stretched (top) position
cues: Thigh pad locked down, hips flexed. Curl from full knee extension to full flexion, squeezing the pad toward the seat each rep. The lengthened hip position makes this great for the 20-30 rep range and lengthened partials. Minimal synergists, so rest can be short.

name: Standing (Single-Leg) Leg Curl
rom_notes: One leg curled at a time against a machine pad or a cable ankle cuff; hip roughly neutral/extended. Knee-flexion isolation per leg, allowing focused mind-muscle connection and unilateral balancing of strength.
regional_bias: unilateral knee-flexion isolation; neutral-hip position sits between the seated (flexed) and lying (extended) hamstring length profiles
cues: Brace the torso upright, curl the heel to the glute one leg at a time without swinging the hips. Full extension to full flexion every rep. Good for correcting left/right imbalances and for cable-cuff setups when no leg-curl machine is available.

name: Barbell Flat Bench Press
rom_notes: Touch the bar to the sternum every rep for full pec stretch; lock out at top without losing scapular retraction. Flat (0 deg) produces homogeneous EMG across all three pec portions and the highest absolute load of the press family.
regional_bias: whole pec (balanced clavicular/sternal/costal); slight sternocostal emphasis vs incline
cues: Retract and depress scapulae, feet planted, slight arch; lower under control to the sternum and pause briefly to protect the chest; drive the bar back over the shoulders. Wider-than-shoulder grip biases pec, narrower biases triceps/front delt.

name: Incline Barbell Bench Press
rom_notes: Set the bench ~30 deg for maximal clavicular (upper) pec EMG; above 45 deg the load shifts substantially to the anterior deltoid and pec EMG drops. Bar touches upper chest/clavicle line. Incline-only training drove the largest 2nd-intercostal (upper pec) thickness gains in trained-naive men.
regional_bias: clavicular (upper) pec; peaks ~30 deg, anterior delt takeover >45 deg
cues: Keep the bench near 30 deg to bias upper pec without over-recruiting the front delt; touch the upper chest, keep elbows ~45-60 deg from torso. Expect lower absolute load than flat.

name: Decline Barbell Bench Press
rom_notes: Decline (~-15 deg) biases the lower/costal (sternocostal) pec and reduces anterior-delt contribution and ROM vs flat. Many lifters already train an unintentional decline via an arched flat bench, so dedicated decline is often redundant.
regional_bias: lower/costal (sternocostal) pec
cues: Secure legs, lower to the lower chest; shorter ROM than flat. Use sparingly since most pressing already biases the lower chest and upper-pec development is the more common limiter.

name: Dumbbell Flat Bench Press
rom_notes: Dumbbells allow a deeper stretch than a barbell by letting the hands travel outside shoulder width below chest level; greater stretch under load is a key pec growth driver. Less stable than barbell, so best trained 10-20 reps.
regional_bias: whole pec, sternocostal emphasis; deep-stretch loaded
cues: Let the dumbbells descend below and outside the chest for a big stretch, then press up and slightly together. Hold a controlled bottom pause. Heavier DBs limit grip/setup, keeping this in moderate reps.

name: Incline Dumbbell Bench Press
rom_notes: Incline (~30 deg) biases clavicular pec; dumbbells add a deeper bottom stretch than the incline barbell. Keep the angle near 30 deg to avoid the anterior-delt takeover seen above 45 deg.
regional_bias: clavicular (upper) pec with deep stretch
cues: Bench at ~30 deg, lower the dumbbells wide and deep, press up and in. A staple upper-pec builder; train in moderate reps for stability and faster-fiber recruitment.

name: Smith Machine Flat Bench Press
rom_notes: Fixed vertical bar path reduces stabilizer demand vs free-weight bench while keeping pec/triceps drive similar; the medial-deltoid stabilizer is the main muscle that differs vs free weights. Useful for pushing close to failure safely.
regional_bias: whole pec (balanced); fixed-path sternocostal
cues: Set bench so the bar tracks to the sternum; the fixed path lets you grind closer to failure. Lower stabilizer demand than a barbell, so loads can run slightly higher.

name: Smith Machine Incline Press
rom_notes: Incline (~30 deg) on a fixed bar path; biases clavicular pec with reduced stabilizer demand. Keep angle near 30 deg to limit anterior-delt dominance.
regional_bias: clavicular (upper) pec
cues: Incline ~30 deg, bar to upper chest, drive straight up the fixed track; good for safely chasing failure on upper-pec work.

name: Machine Chest Press
rom_notes: Seated horizontal press with chest/back support; the fixed path and seat back remove balance demand so it is well-suited to high-rep work (20-30) where barbells/DBs get forearm-limited. Use the fullest ROM the machine allows.
regional_bias: whole pec (mid/sternal); height of handles can shift bias
cues: Set seat height so handles align with mid-chest; press to full extension and allow a deep stretch. Low systemic and grip cost makes it ideal for myoreps, drop sets, and high-rep finishers.

name: Incline Machine Press
rom_notes: Incline-angled seated press biasing clavicular pec with no balance demand; good for high-rep upper-chest work where free weights fatigue the forearms first.
regional_bias: clavicular (upper) pec
cues: Press up and slightly inward, full ROM into a stretch; low grip/systemic cost suits 20-30 rep upper-pec sets and intensity techniques.

name: Dumbbell Flat Flye
rom_notes: Single-joint horizontal adduction with elbows softly fixed; emphasizes the loaded bottom stretch. Train ~10-20 reps (not 5-10) since heavy flyes stress the shoulder in the stretched position. Trains the pec with minimal triceps involvement.
regional_bias: whole pec, stretch-biased (sternal)
cues: Maintain a soft fixed elbow bend, open wide for a deep stretch, then hug the dumbbells together over the chest. Pause at the stretch; never go so heavy you lose control at the bottom.

name: Incline Dumbbell Flye
rom_notes: Incline (~30 deg) single-joint flye biasing the clavicular pec under stretch; isolation movement with negligible triceps demand. Best in moderate-to-high reps for shoulder safety.
regional_bias: clavicular (upper) pec, stretch-biased
cues: Bench ~30 deg, soft elbows, open wide and deep, adduct up and together; pause the stretch and keep the load moderate.

name: Cable Flye (Mid)
rom_notes: Cables keep tension on the pec throughout the adduction arc (unlike dumbbells, which lose tension at the top), allowing full hand-crossover past midline for peak contraction. Pulleys set at mid/shoulder height target the sternal pec.
regional_bias: whole pec (sternal); constant-tension peak contraction
cues: Step forward into a slight stretch, soft elbows, sweep the handles together and cross past midline; squeeze at the end. Low grip/systemic cost makes it a great high-rep finisher.

name: High-to-Low Cable Crossover
rom_notes: Pulleys set high, handles swept down-and-in toward the waist; the downward adduction vector biases the lower/sternocostal pec. Constant cable tension across the full crossover.
regional_bias: lower/sternocostal pec
cues: Stagger stance, soft elbows, pull from high to low and cross the hands in front of the waist; squeeze the lower chest. Light, joint-friendly accessory.

name: Low-to-High Cable Crossover
rom_notes: Pulleys set low, handles swept up-and-in toward chin/clavicle height; the upward adduction vector biases the clavicular (upper) pec with constant cable tension.
regional_bias: clavicular (upper) pec
cues: Soft elbows, sweep from low and wide up to in front of the upper chest; squeeze the upper pec at the top. Joint-friendly upper-chest isolation.

name: Bayesian Cable Flye
rom_notes: Single-arm cable flye performed with the cable behind the body and the shoulder internally rotated (thumb-down), mimicking the bench-press humeral position; loads the pec deep in the stretched/behind-the-body range. Henselmans-favored isolation.
regional_bias: whole pec, deep-stretch biased; matches pressing internal-rotation pattern
cues: Cable from behind, internally rotate so the palm/thumb faces down, let the arm travel back into a deep stretch, then adduct across the body. One arm at a time for full ROM and a strong stretch loaded.

name: Pec Deck Machine Flye
rom_notes: Fixed-arc horizontal adduction against pads; the seat-back support removes any synergist/balance demand, so rest periods can be very short (no synergist recovery needed). Pure pec isolation with no grip or triceps cost.
regional_bias: whole pec (sternal); isolation
cues: Set seat so pads align with mid-chest; drive elbows/forearms together and squeeze, control the stretch back. Excellent for myoreps, drop sets, and pre-exhaust supersets given its very low fatigue and grip cost.

name: Chest Dip
rom_notes: Forward torso lean and flared elbows turn the dip into a lower/sternocostal pec emphasis (a vertical, decline-like adduction); deep stretch at the bottom. Can be loaded via dip belt with a hung plate. Joint-stressful at the bottom for many lifters.
regional_bias: lower/sternocostal pec (with forward lean)
cues: Lean the torso forward, flare elbows out, descend until you feel a deep chest stretch, then press up and in. Add load with a dip belt. Stop short if it aggravates the shoulder/elbow.

name: Push-Up
rom_notes: Closed-chain horizontal press; matched-EMG push-ups produce strength gains comparable to the bench press. Free scapulae (not pinned to a bench) let the shoulder blades move naturally, which many find more shoulder-friendly, and add serratus anterior demand. A standard push-up is effectively a slight decline press.
regional_bias: whole pec (lower bias); serratus-loaded via protraction
cues: Rigid plank, hands ~shoulder width, lower the chest to the floor, then press and protract (push the floor away) at the top to load the serratus. Let the scapulae move freely.

name: Weighted Push-Up
rom_notes: Push-up loaded with a plate on the back or a resistance band across the shoulders to keep reps in a productive hypertrophy range as bodyweight alone becomes too easy. Same closed-chain, free-scapula benefits as the push-up.
regional_bias: whole pec (lower bias); serratus-loaded
cues: Add a plate on the upper back (or band) to overload; keep a rigid plank, full ROM to the floor, protract hard at lockout. A high-rep machine-press alternative when forearm endurance is not the limiter.

name: Dumbbell Decline Bench Press
rom_notes: Decline (~-15 deg) dumbbell press biasing the lower/costal pec with a deeper stretch than the barbell decline and reduced anterior-delt contribution. Often redundant with already lower-chest-biased flat pressing.
regional_bias: lower/costal (sternocostal) pec, deep stretch
cues: Secure legs, lower the dumbbells wide and deep on the lower chest, press up and together. Use selectively since most pressing already favors the lower chest.

name: Machine Crunch
rom_notes: Load the full spinal flexion arc: start with the lumbar/thoracic spine extended over the pad so the rectus is stretched, then crunch torso past perpendicular. Stretch under load drives growth; do not shorten the top by jerking.
regional_bias: whole rectus abdominis (loadable across all rep ranges)
cues: Flex the spine, not the hips; round the back over the pad. Pause and squeeze the abs hard at the bottom of the crunch. Slow the eccentric to keep tension off the hip flexors.

name: Cable Crunch (Kneeling Rope Crunch)
rom_notes: Hips stay fixed (do not turn it into a hip hinge); crunch the rib cage toward the pelvis. Let the cable pull the spine into extension at the top for a loaded stretch, then curl down vertebra by vertebra.
regional_bias: upper and mid rectus abdominis
cues: Keep the hips locked and bend only at the spine. Pull elbows toward thighs by rounding the upper back, not by sitting back. Resist the eccentric to maintain a deep stretch at the top.

name: Weighted Crunch (Plate / Dumbbell on Chest)
rom_notes: Lie supine, ideally over a slight back extension (rolled towel or decline) so the spine can extend at the start; crunch the torso up by flexing the spine, not by hinging at the hip.
regional_bias: upper rectus abdominis
cues: Hold the plate against the chest or extended overhead to add resistance. Curl the shoulders toward the hips, exhaling as you flex. Don't yank the neck; let the abs do the work.

name: Decline / Slant-Board Sit-Up
rom_notes: RP cue: lay all the way back relaxed at the start of each rep and come up past perpendicular to the ground for a full ab stretch and contraction. Restricting ROM hides ab weakness. Decline angle increases hip-flexor involvement vs. flat sit-up.
regional_bias: whole rectus abdominis, hip-flexor co-contribution
cues: Lay back until the abs are fully stretched, then roll up by flexing the spine first before the hips. Slow the movement so you flex the spine rather than just cranking with the hip flexors. Add a plate on the chest to load into lower rep ranges.

name: AbMat Sit-Up
rom_notes: The AbMat under the lumbar spine allows extension below the floor line at the start, increasing the stretched-position ROM of the rectus before flexing up past vertical.
regional_bias: whole rectus abdominis, emphasis on lengthened range
cues: Extend back over the mat to deepen the stretch, then sit up by curling the spine. Reach the hands past the knees at the top to ensure full flexion. Hold a plate overhead to load.

name: Reaching Sit-Up
rom_notes: RP staple light/high-rep move: lay fully back, then sit up reaching the arms forward and overhead past the knees, emphasizing a full spinal flexion under bodyweight. Naturally falls in the 10-20+ rep range.
regional_bias: whole rectus abdominis
cues: Reach the fingertips toward and past the toes at the top to force complete flexion. Lay all the way back between reps to expand the abs. Low-fatigue exercise, well-suited to high frequency and myoreps.

name: Hanging Leg Raise
rom_notes: Dead-hang from the bar with straight legs; raise legs to horizontal then curl the pelvis up (posterior tilt) to roll the lumbar spine and bias the rectus over pure hip flexion. The posterior pelvic tilt at the top is what makes it an ab exercise rather than only hip-flexor work. Grip endurance can limit set length.
regional_bias: lower rectus abdominis
cues: Hang without swinging; raise the legs then tuck the pelvis under to curl the lower abs. Control the descent rather than dropping the legs. If grip fails before the abs, use straps or switch to a captain's-chair leg raise.

name: Hanging Knee Raise
rom_notes: Dead-hang from the bar; raise bent knees toward the chest then posteriorly tilt the pelvis to curl the lumbar spine. Shorter lever than the straight-leg raise, so easier and naturally higher-rep (RP programs it in 20-30).
regional_bias: lower rectus abdominis
cues: Drive the knees up and roll the hips under at the top to flex the spine. Avoid kipping or swinging. Lower under control to a full hang. Grip is often the limiter; use straps if it fails before the abs.

name: Captain's Chair Leg Raise
rom_notes: Forearm-supported on the pads removes the grip limiter of the hanging version, letting the abs be trained to failure. Raise legs and posteriorly tilt the pelvis to curl the lower spine.
regional_bias: lower rectus abdominis
cues: Press the back flat into the pad and tuck the pelvis under to curl the lower abs, not just lift the legs. Control the descent. Add ankle weights or hold a dumbbell between the feet to load.

name: Lying Leg Raise
rom_notes: Supine on the floor or bench; raise straight legs to vertical then lift the hips off the floor (posterior tilt) to curl the lumbar spine. Keeping the low back pressed down protects the spine and keeps tension on the rectus.
regional_bias: lower rectus abdominis
cues: Press the low back into the floor throughout; finish each rep with a small hip-lift to curl the lower abs. Lower the legs only as far as you can without the low back arching. Slow the eccentric.

name: Reverse Crunch
rom_notes: Supine with knees bent ~90deg; curl the pelvis up toward the rib cage so the lumbar spine flexes and the hips roll off the floor. Minimal hip flexion means it isolates the lower rectus via posterior pelvic tilt better than a leg raise.
regional_bias: lower rectus abdominis
cues: Curl the hips up and in, rolling the pelvis toward the ribs rather than swinging the legs. Pause and squeeze at the top. Lower slowly to keep the lower abs under tension. Perform on a decline bench to load the lengthened range.

name: V-Up
rom_notes: Simultaneously raise straight legs and torso to meet over the hips, folding the body into a V. RP notes V-Ups can be tough to load heavily but are excellent for myoreps to hit faster fibers; very challenging variations fall into the 5-10 range.
regional_bias: whole rectus abdominis (upper + lower simultaneously)
cues: Fold torso and legs together to meet over the hips, reaching the hands to the toes. Fully extend and lay back between reps for a stretch. Hard to load, so use myoreps for fast-fiber stimulus.

name: Candlestick / Modified Candlestick
rom_notes: RP's heaviest bodyweight ab move: from supine, roll up bringing straight legs overhead/vertical and curl the spine maximally, then control the descent. A small technique change causes big rep differences, so RP recommends giant sets to dial in technique. Naturally a 5-10 rep heavy movement.
regional_bias: whole rectus abdominis, lengthened-range emphasis
cues: Curl the spine to roll up, keeping legs together and controlled (do not throw them). Resist the eccentric to a full lay-back stretch. Use giant sets to perfect technique since small changes swing the reps a lot.

name: Ab-Wheel Rollout
rom_notes: Anti-extension: the abs work isometrically (with a large eccentric demand) to resist lumbar extension as the wheel rolls away and the body lengthens into a stretched, near-prone position, then concentrically pull back. The lengthened bottom position loads the rectus under deep stretch. Progress from knees to standing.
regional_bias: whole rectus abdominis, lengthened-range bias
cues: Brace hard and tuck the pelvis so the low back never sags into extension. Roll out only as far as you can keep the spine neutral, then pull back with the abs (not the hips). Keep the lats engaged to assist the return.

name: Plank (Front Plank)
rom_notes: Isometric anti-extension hold: the abs resist gravity collapsing the lumbar spine into extension. No ROM; scored by time under tension. Limited as a hypertrophy tool (isometric, low loadability) but a core staple. Load by adding a plate on the back or elevating feet (RKC plank ups intensity).
regional_bias: whole anterior core, transversus emphasis
cues: Squeeze glutes and tuck the pelvis to flatten the low back; do not let the hips sag. Keep a straight line from head to heels. Add a plate on the upper back to progress, or do an RKC plank (maximal full-body tension) for a harder, shorter hold.

name: Weighted Plank
rom_notes: Front plank with a plate (or chains) loaded on the upper back to increase the anti-extension demand and bring the hold into a strength-relevant time range. RP mentions weighted plank holds as a (rare) compound-style ab target, e.g. paired in a pre-exhaust superset.
regional_bias: whole anterior core, transversus emphasis
cues: Have a partner place a plate across the upper back/hips. Brace and tuck the pelvis; resist the extra load pulling the low back into extension. Keep breathing shallow but steady through the hold.

name: Cable Pallof Press
rom_notes: Anti-rotation: stand side-on to a cable, press the handle straight out from the sternum; the obliques resist the cable's pull to rotate the trunk. Pressing out lengthens the lever and peaks the rotational torque. Isometric-dominant resistance, minimal spinal ROM.
regional_bias: obliques (anti-rotation), bilateral bracing
cues: Square the hips and shoulders; do not let the torso twist toward the stack. Press the handle straight out and hold, resisting rotation, then return. Brace the whole trunk; the resistance is the cable trying to turn you.

name: Cable Woodchop (High-to-Low / Low-to-High)
rom_notes: Dynamic trunk rotation/diagonal flexion driven by the obliques, chopping the handle across the body from high-to-low or low-to-high. Unlike the Pallof, this is concentric oblique rotation through ROM. Rotation should come mostly from the thoracic spine/trunk with the hips pivoting, keeping the lumbar spine relatively safe.
regional_bias: obliques (rotation), diagonal anterior core
cues: Drive the chop with the abs and obliques, pivoting the back foot; let the arms follow rather than lead. Rotate through the trunk, not the low back. Control the return so the obliques work eccentrically.

name: Dumbbell Side Bend
rom_notes: Frontal-plane trunk work (mapped to the leaf's anti-lateral-flexion pattern as the closest QL/oblique frontal-plane slot, though the loaded side bend is concentric lateral flexion, not purely anti-): hold a DB in one hand, bend laterally toward it for a stretch on the opposite QL/obliques, then crunch back up sideways. Train the contralateral side under load; the holding-side obliques/QL work as the prime movers.
regional_bias: obliques and quadratus lumborum (lateral chain)
cues: Hold the DB in one hand and bend straight sideways (no forward lean or twist). Let it pull you into a deep lateral stretch, then bend back up by crunching the opposite obliques. Keep the load on the working side; one DB only.

name: Cable Side Bend
rom_notes: Same frontal-plane lateral-flexion movement as the DB version but with a low-pulley handle, giving more constant tension through the stretched range. Bend toward the stack for the stretch, then laterally flex back up against the cable.
regional_bias: obliques and quadratus lumborum (lateral chain)
cues: Stand side-on to a low pulley; bend toward the stack for a deep lateral stretch, then crunch sideways away from it. Move only in the frontal plane, no twisting. Constant cable tension keeps the obliques loaded at full stretch.

name: Suitcase Carry
rom_notes: Loaded carry with weight in one hand; the contralateral QL/obliques fire isometrically (anti-lateral-flexion) to keep the torso upright against the offset load while walking. The closed hand is loaded under heavy tension (load hangs from the grip), so it carries crush-grip and weight-hanging tags. Scored by distance/time, not reps.
regional_bias: quadratus lumborum and obliques (anti-lateral-flexion), grip
cues: Hold one heavy DB/KB and walk tall; resist leaning toward or away from the load. Keep shoulders and hips level and the trunk braced. Grip is a co-limiter; use a thick or heavy handle to also tax the crush grip. Switch hands each set.

name: Standing Barbell Overhead Press
rom_notes: Bar from clavicle/upper-chest height pressed to lockout overhead; lower at least until bar touches clavicle/shoulders. Standing version loads the core and erectors heavily for stabilization.
regional_bias: anterior deltoid (also lateral deltoid when elbows flared); high systemic/core cost
tempo: controlled eccentric, brief pause at shoulders
cues: Squeeze glutes and brace to keep ribs down; press the bar back over the mid-foot once it clears the face; full lockout with traps shrugging up at the top.

name: Seated Barbell Overhead Press
rom_notes: Pressed from upper chest to lockout against a back-supported bench; the back pad removes most erector/core stabilization demand vs standing so more load reaches the delts.
regional_bias: anterior deltoid; lower systemic cost than standing variant
cues: Keep a moderate upright back angle; do not over-arch into a quasi-incline-press; lower to clavicle each rep.

name: Seated Dumbbell Shoulder Press
rom_notes: Dumbbells allow a deeper stretch at the bottom (lower than a bar past the clavicle) which more strongly taxes the front delts; each arm works independently so no bar to balance.
regional_bias: anterior deltoid with deep-stretch emphasis
tempo: controlled eccentric into a deep bottom stretch
cues: Lower the dumbbells until your hands are at shoulder/ear height for a deep stretch; keep wrists stacked over elbows; can self-spot by kneeing the bells up.

name: Smith Machine Seated Shoulder Press
rom_notes: Fixed vertical bar path removes the balance demand; pressed from clavicle to lockout. Lower stabilization cost makes it a good high-rep / late-block press option.
regional_bias: anterior deltoid; low systemic disruption (good for higher reps)
cues: Set the bench so the bar tracks just in front of your face; touch the clavicle each rep; the fixed path lets you push close to failure safely.

name: Machine Shoulder Press
rom_notes: Guided handle path from shoulder height to lockout against a chest/back pad; minimal balance or core demand, making it ideal for 20-30 rep front-delt pump work without tiring the core.
regional_bias: anterior deltoid; lowest systemic cost of the presses
cues: Adjust the seat so handles start at shoulder height; press to a soft lockout; great for high-rep pump sets and pre-exhaust supersets where core stays fresh.

name: Dumbbell Lateral Raise
rom_notes: Arms abduct from the sides up to ~shoulder height; the bottom half is the most growth-promoting portion (peak tension where the lever arm is long). Pulling above the horizontal is optional and only if pain-free. Resistance is lowest at the bottom (gravity), so the loaded stretch is weak vs cable.
regional_bias: lateral (middle) deltoid; raising in the true frontal plane minimizes front-delt takeover vs scapular-plane raising
cues: Lead with the elbows, not the hands; raise in the frontal plane (not 30deg forward) to bias the lateral fibers; control the negative rather than dropping.

name: Cable Lateral Raise
rom_notes: Cable from a low pulley keeps tension constant across the whole arc, including the bottom stretched position where a dumbbell has almost none; usually done one arm at a time, often cross-body for a deeper stretch.
regional_bias: lateral deltoid with strong loaded-stretch emphasis at the bottom
cues: Stand so the cable line stays roughly perpendicular to the upper arm at the top; let the arm draw across the midline at the bottom for a deeper stretch; drive the elbow up and out.

name: Cable Cross-Body Lateral Raise
rom_notes: Low pulley set across the body; the arm starts fully adducted across the front of the torso (deep stretch on the lateral delt) and abducts out and up. Maximizes the loaded stretch position RP highlights as the lead side-delt exercise.
regional_bias: lateral deltoid, loaded-stretch biased
tempo: slow controlled eccentric into the cross-body stretch
cues: Reach the working hand all the way across to the opposite hip at the bottom; abduct up and out to shoulder height; keep the torso still and let the delt do the work.

name: Machine Lateral Raise
rom_notes: Pads on the outer upper arm guide pure shoulder abduction with the load applied at the elbow/arm rather than the hand, so grip is bypassed entirely. Often has no real synergist, allowing very short rest and myorep/drop-set use.
regional_bias: lateral deltoid; grip- and core-free so ideal for high-rep, myorep, and drop work
cues: Set the pivot at the shoulder joint; push against the pads with the upper arm, not the hands; perfect candidate for myoreps since there is no limiting synergist and grip is bypassed.

name: Lean-Away Dumbbell Lateral Raise
rom_notes: Holding a post and leaning away shifts the dumbbell's resistance arm so the bottom (stretched) position is loaded rather than the top, addressing the dumbbell lateral's weak-bottom problem. One arm at a time.
regional_bias: lateral deltoid with bottom/stretch emphasis
cues: Grab a rack upright and lean so the working arm hangs across the body; raise to shoulder height; the lean makes the bottom of the rep the hardest part.

name: Barbell Upright Row
rom_notes: Bar pulled vertically from thigh/waist toward upper chest with elbows leading high; one of the few side-delt exercises that loads heavily enough for the 5-10 rep range. Pull only as high as is pain-free; a narrower pull and lower height reduce impingement risk.
regional_bias: lateral deltoid and upper trapezius (more trap as the pull goes higher / wider abduction)
cues: Lead with the elbows above the wrists; pull to roughly nipple/chin height only if pain-free; mind-muscle connection is hard here so it is a poor myorep choice but good for heavier loading.

name: Dumbbell Upright Row
rom_notes: Dumbbells let each arm drift to a more natural path, reducing wrist/shoulder strain vs the fixed bar; pulled from the thighs up toward the chest, elbows leading. Slightly lighter loading than the barbell version, used as a moderate-rep rotation.
regional_bias: lateral deltoid and upper trapezius
cues: Keep the dumbbells close to the body; lead with high elbows; let the path stay comfortable for the wrists since they aren't locked to a bar.

name: Cable Upright Row
rom_notes: Low pulley keeps continuous tension through the pull; lighter, smoother loading makes it a good light/high-rep (20-30) upright-row option. Rope attachment allows the wrists to externally rotate at the top, easing shoulder stress.
regional_bias: lateral deltoid and upper trapezius
cues: Stand close to the pulley; lead with high elbows; use a rope to let the hands split apart at the top and spare the shoulders; ideal for higher-rep light work.

name: Dumbbell Front Raise
rom_notes: Arm flexes from the side/front of the thigh up to ~shoulder height (or slightly above) in the sagittal plane. Isolation for the front delt; rarely needed since pressing and chest work already cover the anterior deltoid heavily.
regional_bias: anterior deltoid
cues: Raise to about shoulder height without leaning back or swinging; lower under control; useful mainly as pre-exhaust before pressing if front delts are a priority.

name: Cable Front Raise
rom_notes: Low pulley behind/beside the body keeps tension constant from the bottom stretch through the top; flex the arm forward to shoulder height. Cable line makes drop sets easy, which RP notes work well here.
regional_bias: anterior deltoid, continuous-tension
cues: Take the pulley from a low position so tension holds at the bottom; raise to shoulder height; strip the stack for easy drop sets.

name: Cable Face Pull
rom_notes: Rope pulled from a high/eye-level pulley toward the face with the elbows flaring high and wide, ending in external rotation. Continuous cable tension and a clear stretch make it RP's top rear-delt pick; also trains the rotator cuff and mid-traps.
regional_bias: posterior deltoid plus external rotators (infraspinatus/teres minor) and mid-trap
tempo: controlled, pause at peak with external rotation
cues: Pull the rope to your forehead with elbows high and wide; finish by rotating the knuckles up and back; pause and squeeze the rear delts at the top since the back can easily take over.

name: Reverse Pec-Deck (Machine Rear Delt Fly)
rom_notes: Chest against the pad, arms sweep from in front of the body out to the sides in pure horizontal abduction. Load is taken at the arms/handles with chest support, so it is grip- and core-light; consistent tension and a near-absent synergist make it great for high-rep, myorep, and pre-exhaust work.
regional_bias: posterior deltoid; minimal synergist so rest can be very short
cues: Use a slight elbow bend and sweep the arms straight back, not down; pause and feel the rear delts at the back; ideal for myoreps and as a pre-exhaust before face pulls or rows.

name: Bent-Over Dumbbell Rear Lateral Raise
rom_notes: Hinged at the hips, arms hang down and sweep out to the sides (horizontal abduction relative to the torso). Free-weight version has little tension at the bottom, so going fully down each rep is optional; a top pause greatly improves the mind-muscle connection. Mind-muscle connection is poor in the 5-10 range, so use moderate-to-light loads.
regional_bias: posterior deltoid
cues: Hinge so the torso is near parallel; raise the dumbbells out to the sides leading with the elbows; pause and squeeze at the top since the back/traps love to take over; keep it light enough to feel the rear delts.

name: Cable Cross-Body Rear Lateral Raise
rom_notes: Single arm pulls across the body from a pulley on the opposite side, starting fully adducted (deep stretch on the rear delt) and sweeping out into horizontal abduction. Maximizes the loaded stretch RP and Henselmans prize for the rear delt; constant cable tension throughout.
regional_bias: posterior deltoid, loaded-stretch biased
tempo: slow eccentric into the cross-body stretch
cues: Set the pulley about shoulder height across your body; let the arm draw fully across for a deep stretch; sweep it back and out, leading with the back of the hand.

name: Cable Cuff Lateral Raise (Grip-Bypass)
rom_notes: A wrist cuff attaches the cable to the wrist instead of a handle, removing all grip/finger-flexor demand so the lateral delt is the sole limiting factor. Same constant-tension abduction arc as a cable lateral; ideal when grip is the bottleneck (e.g. after heavy pulling) or for pure isolation.
regional_bias: lateral deltoid; grip fully bypassed
cues: Strap the cuff around the wrist and let the hand stay relaxed; abduct the upper arm without gripping anything; perfect for myoreps/drops and for trainees whose grip fatigues before the delt.

name: Cable Cuff Rear Delt Fly (Grip-Bypass)
rom_notes: Wrist cuff removes grip demand so the rear delt is the only limiting factor through a constant-tension horizontal-abduction arc; can be done cross-body for a deep stretch. Useful for grip-bypass isolation and for very-short-rest myorep/drop work.
regional_bias: posterior deltoid; grip fully bypassed
cues: Cuff the wrist and keep the hand open; sweep the upper arm back and out without gripping; pause at the peak to lock in the rear-delt connection.

name: Barbell Bent-Over Row (Overhand)
rom_notes: Hinged torso ~15-45deg from horizontal; bar from arms fully extended (deep stretch of lats/mid-back) to lower-chest/upper-abdomen contact. RP: full ROM, no swinging — only legs/torso bounce add momentum, not target stimulus. Avoid the trap of only training the mid-range.
regional_bias: whole upper/mid back; overhand + flared elbows biases upper back, rhomboids, mid-traps and rear delt
cues: Brace the lower back hard in the hinge; pull the bar to the lower chest/upper abdomen with elbows out; do not let the torso rise to heave the weight (RP: ~95% of bent rows are cheated). Best in the 5-20 rep range — at 20-30 the lower back fatigues before the back does.

name: Barbell Bent-Over Row (with Lifting Straps)
rom_notes: Same ROM as overhand barbell row; straps transfer load from the fingers to the wrist so grip no longer caps the heavy back work, letting the lats/mid-back reach failure first.
regional_bias: whole upper/mid back; grip removed as limiter so target back muscles drive failure
cues: Wrap straps so part of the weight is borne by the wrist, not the closed fingers (straps review/bench-pull: workload transfers from forearm flexors to the strap anchor). Grip-assist matters most when absolute loads are high, as in the heavy row — for lighter pulls the strap benefit shrinks.

name: Pendlay Row (Dead-Stop Barbell Row)
rom_notes: Torso held near-horizontal/parallel to floor; bar resets on the floor each rep (dead stop), eliminating the stretch-reflex and forcing a concentric-dominant explosive pull to the lower chest.
regional_bias: explosive upper-back / mid-trap and rhomboid emphasis; strict torso angle limits cheating
cues: Reset the bar fully on the floor each rep, keep the torso parallel and motionless, pull explosively to the lower chest. The dead stop enforces strict technique RP says most bent rows lack. Pair best with heavy 5-10 rep work.

name: Barbell Row (Underhand / Supinated Grip)
rom_notes: Supinated grip drives a tighter, more tucked elbow path so the bar travels to the lower abdomen; longer stretch on the lats at the bottom, biceps more loaded than overhand.
regional_bias: lower lats and teres major via the tucked, elbows-back path; greater biceps contribution
cues: Supinate the grip, drive the elbows down and back toward the hips to bias the lats. Henselmans: an elbows-back row path emphasizes the lats/teres major versus the flared high-row that hits upper back and rear delt.

name: T-Bar Row (Landmine Row)
rom_notes: Barbell anchored in a landmine/T-bar pad; neutral close grip on a V-handle, hinged torso, pull plate to chest/abdomen. Neutral grip allows a deep stretch and big mid-back contraction; arc is fixed by the pivot.
regional_bias: thick mid-back — rhomboids, mid-traps, teres major; neutral grip lets heavy loading with comfortable shoulder/wrist positions
cues: Hinge and brace the lumbar spine, pull the handle into the lower chest with elbows moderately tucked. Wide-grip handle shifts toward upper back/rear delt; narrow neutral handle biases lats and mid-back.

name: Chest-Supported Row (Machine / Plate-Loaded)
rom_notes: Torso braced on an angled chest pad removes lower-back/erector demand and cheating; arms move from full forward stretch to elbows-back contraction. Pad lets you let the shoulder blades drift forward at the bottom for extra stretch.
regional_bias: mid-back and lats with minimal lower-back fatigue; high SFR because torso support removes the limiting stabilizers
cues: Keep the chest pinned to the pad, protract at the bottom to lengthen the back, then drive elbows back and squeeze. Because the lower back is unloaded, this works well up into the 20-30 rep range where free barbell rows would fatigue the spine first (RP).

name: Incline-Bench Chest-Supported Dumbbell Row
rom_notes: Chest braced on a 30-45deg incline bench; dumbbells hang at full stretch and row up and back. Free dumbbells allow a slightly longer ROM and let the scapulae drift forward at the bottom; load is hand-held so grip is engaged.
regional_bias: mid-back/lats with no lower-back demand; neutral or pronated grip selectable to shift between lat and upper-back bias
cues: Lie chest-down on the incline, let the dumbbells stretch the lats fully at the bottom, row with elbows back for lats or flared for upper back. Dumbbells are gripped, so without straps the closed hand is loaded under tension.

name: One-Arm Dumbbell Row (Bench-Supported)
rom_notes: One hand and knee braced on a bench; working-side dumbbell from a deep hanging stretch to the hip with a long ROM. Unilateral setup allows the elbow to travel far back and the torso to be fully supported.
regional_bias: lats and teres major via a long elbows-back pull; per-side loading lets you bias each lat individually
cues: Brace on the bench, let the shoulder blade protract and the dumbbell drop into a deep stretch, then drive the elbow back to the hip. The dumbbell hangs from the closed hand under load, so grip is taxed without straps.

name: Seated Cable Row (Wide Pronated Grip)
rom_notes: Seated, wide pronated bar; pull to the upper abdomen/lower chest with flared elbows. Cable keeps constant tension; allow the scapulae to protract forward at the bottom for full mid-back stretch.
regional_bias: upper back — rhomboids, mid-traps and rear delt — via the wide, elbows-flared high-row path
cues: Keep the torso fairly upright, flare the elbows and pull the wide bar to the upper abdomen, squeezing the shoulder blades. Henselmans: flared, high-row elbow path biases upper back and rear delt over the lats.

name: Seated Cable Row (Close Neutral V-Handle)
rom_notes: Seated with a close neutral V-handle; elbows tuck and drive back to the lower abdomen for a lat-biased path. Constant cable tension; long protracted stretch at the front.
regional_bias: lats and teres major via the close, elbows-tucked-and-back pull
cues: Lean back only slightly, let the handle stretch the lats forward, then pull the elbows down and back tight to the body. The close neutral grip and tucked elbows shift emphasis to the lats versus the wide high-row.

name: Single-Arm Seated/Half-Kneeling Cable Row
rom_notes: Single D-handle pulled per side; the cable allows the shoulder blade to protract and reach forward at the front, giving a longer lat stretch and rotational reach than a fixed bar. Trunk resists the cable's pull (anti-rotation demand).
regional_bias: lats/teres major with extra range; allows independent per-side reach and scapular protraction at the stretch
cues: Reach across and let the shoulder blade come forward for a deep stretch, then row the elbow back while resisting trunk rotation. The free single handle lets the back work through a longer arc than a fixed bar.

name: Iso-Lateral / Hammer Strength Plate-Loaded Row
rom_notes: Chest-supported plate-loaded machine with a fixed pulling arc; handles can be pulled together or one arm at a time. Pad removes lower-back demand; converging arc allows a strong contraction with a guided groove.
regional_bias: mid-back and lats; handle height/grip selects upper-back versus lat bias; very high SFR for a low-skill, low-systemic-fatigue row
cues: Chest on the pad, full stretch forward, drive the handles back and squeeze. RP recommends adding less systemically disruptive moves like machine rows later in a block — low fatigue, easy to push to 20-30 reps.

name: Meadows Row (Landmine Single-Arm Row)
rom_notes: Single-arm pull on the end of a landmine-anchored barbell, staggered stance, hinged torso. The landmine arc gives a long stretch at the bottom and a pronated overhand grip on the sleeve.
regional_bias: lats and teres major, with strong upper-back involvement; pronated grip plus the landmine arc loads the stretched position heavily
cues: Stagger the stance, hinge and brace, grip the barbell sleeve overhand and pull from a deep stretch up to the hip. Heavy pronated single-arm hold means the closed hand is loaded — taxing without straps.

name: Inverted Row (Bodyweight Horizontal Row)
rom_notes: Body suspended under a fixed bar or rings; pull the chest to the bar from full arm extension. ROM and difficulty scale with body angle (more horizontal = harder); trunk braced as a rigid plank throughout.
regional_bias: upper/mid back and rear delt; difficulty self-regulated by foot position, good for higher-rep upper-back work
cues: Keep a rigid plank from heels to head, pull the chest to the bar and squeeze the shoulder blades. Lower the feet or elevate them to scale load; can be weighted with a vest or plate once bodyweight is easy.

name: Gorilla Row (Bent-Over Alternating Dumbbell Row)
rom_notes: Two dumbbells rest on the floor between the feet; hinge and row one arm at a time to the hip while the other supports. Free-standing hinge means the torso is unsupported and the erectors and trunk brace hard.
regional_bias: lats and teres major with anti-rotation trunk demand; alternating single-arm loading lets each side be driven hard
cues: Hinge with a flat braced back, row one dumbbell to the hip while resisting trunk twist, then alternate. Heavy dumbbells held in the closed hand under load make grip a real demand without straps.

name: Seal Row (Prone Bench Barbell/Dumbbell Row)
rom_notes: Lying prone on a raised flat bench (the prone bench pull setup); weight hangs straight down and is rowed to the bench underside. Body fully supported, so all momentum and lower-back/leg drive is eliminated — pure strict back work.
regional_bias: whole mid/upper back with zero cheat; grip strength is the main non-back limiter, which straps can remove
cues: Lie chest-down on the elevated bench, let the weight hang to a full stretch, row strictly to the bench. In the strapped prone bench pull, grip ceases to be the limiter so the back fails first; without straps the closed hand is loaded under tension.

name: High Row / Cable Rear-Delt Row (Elbows-Flared)
rom_notes: Cable set high or at face height; pull toward the upper chest/face with the elbows kept high and flared wide so the upper arm moves in horizontal abduction. Let the scapulae drift forward at the bottom for an upper-back stretch.
regional_bias: rear delt, mid-traps and rhomboids — the elbows-high flared path Henselmans flags for upper-back/rear-delt bias rather than lats
cues: Keep the elbows high and pull them wide and back, leading with the upper arm not the hand. Henselmans: high rows with flared elbows hit the upper back and rear delt; letting the shoulder blades drift forward at the bottom adds stretch.

name: Smith Machine Bent-Over Row
rom_notes: Bar runs on the Smith's fixed vertical track; hinged torso, pull to the lower chest. The guided path removes the need to balance/stabilize the bar so you can chase the back without skill demand; ROM capped by the track.
regional_bias: whole mid/upper back; fixed bar path standardizes the stroke and removes stabilization, akin to the Smith prone bench pull used in strap research
cues: Set a stable hinge, pull the bar straight up the track to the lower chest. The bar is gripped in the closed hand under load, so grip is taxed unless straps are used; the Smith machine's fixed path is what the bench-pull strap study used.

name: High-Bar Back Squat
rom_notes: Bar on traps keeps a more upright torso so the femur drives forward and the knee travels well past the toes, producing greater knee flexion and a deeper, more quad-biased squat than low-bar. RP: go butt-to-calves deep — quad growth lives in the painful bottom stretch. Total knee+hip extensor demand peaks at parallel femur and is fixed for a given load regardless of bar/stance, but high-bar shifts the share toward the knee.
regional_bias: overall quads with rectus femoris emphasis vs low-bar; deep ROM loads vastii at long length
cues: Brace hard, sit straight down between the feet, let the knees travel forward over the toes, hit depth every rep, drive evenly up. Olympic shoes help you stay upright and reach depth.

name: Low-Bar Back Squat
rom_notes: Bar on rear delts forces more torso lean and hip-back travel, increasing the hip-extensor share and reducing knee travel/quad demand relative to high-bar. Lets you move the most weight but is the least quad-biased back-squat variant; still a knee-dominant bilateral squat.
regional_bias: more glute/hip; least rectus-femoris of the squat variants
cues: Bar across the rear delts, wrists straight, big chest. Sit hips back into the hole, keep the bar over midfoot. More hip hinge than high-bar — expect more glute/back contribution.

name: Front Squat
rom_notes: Front-rack load demands a near-vertical torso, maximizing knee travel and forward knee flexion — the most quad-dominant barbell squat. Upright trunk also taxes the erectors and abs to resist flexion. Front-rack grip is hard on wrists; arms-crossed or strap hold is an acceptable substitute for non-weightlifters.
regional_bias: strongest quad bias of the barbell squats; rectus femoris and vastii
cues: Elbows high to keep the thoracic spine extended and build the rack shelf, keep as many fingers on the bar as you can. Stay vertical, knees forward, drop straight down to depth.

name: Machine Hack Squat
rom_notes: Back-supported sled removes balance/postural limits so you can chase deep knee flexion and load the bottom stretch hard. RP: bring stance in and down on the platform to deepen knee travel and quad bias (costs some load). Best in the 5-15 range because it relies on postural support less than a free squat but more than a leg press. Shoulder pads support load — no grip demand.
regional_bias: vastii-dominant; strong quad bias with deep ROM
cues: Feet lower and narrower on the platform for max knee travel, descend until knees pass chest level, control the stretch, don't bounce. Push through the whole foot.

name: Smith Machine Squat
rom_notes: Fixed bar path lets you place the feet forward and stay upright, biasing the quads while removing balance demand. RP groups it just below squats in loading priority and ideal for the 5-15 range. Bar rests on the back, hands only stabilize — low grip demand.
regional_bias: quad-biased; vastii and rectus femoris
cues: Set the feet slightly forward of the bar so you can stay vertical and load the quads. Sit straight down, hit depth, drive up. The fixed path lets you push the stretch safely.

name: Leg Press
rom_notes: Fully supported back and hips remove postural/axial fatigue, giving the widest range of safe-and-effective loads and rep ranges (RP runs it 10-30). Go deep enough that knees track just lateral to the chest with a tight lower back to load the bottom stretch. Lowest systemic cost of the compound presses, so RP adds it later in a block. No grip involvement.
regional_bias: vastii-dominant quad work; foot position shifts adductor involvement
cues: Bring the sled down until your knees come outside your chest, keep your lower back glued to the pad, don't let it round. Push through midfoot. Vary foot stance across mesocycles to hit the adductors too.

name: Single-Leg Leg Press
rom_notes: One leg at a time on the leg press, fully supported, allowing deep knee flexion and a long-length quad stretch per side with minimal balance demand. Useful for fixing side-to-side imbalances; rotatable accessory rather than a routine anchor. No grip demand.
regional_bias: per-side vastii-dominant quad work
cues: Center one foot on the platform, drop the sled deep so the knee tracks toward the same-side shoulder, keep the hips down. Match reps and depth on both sides.

name: Leg Extension
rom_notes: Open-chain knee extension isolating the quads with no synergists, so it can hit portions of the quad that squats miss and tolerates very high reps (RP: 10-30, knees protest under heavy low-rep loads). Standard seated machine sits the hips near 90 degrees, which shortens the biarticular rectus femoris. Typically misses ~40-50 degrees of bottom knee-flexion stretch vs a sissy/reverse-nordic. Pad on the shin, no grip demand. Ideal for myoreps/drop sets/occlusion because it has no limiting synergists.
regional_bias: all four heads; 90-degree hip seating biases the vastii (esp. vastus lateralis) over rectus femoris
cues: Control the lowering, get a full stretch at the bottom, drive to lockout and pause. Keep reps moderate-to-high to spare the knees. Pairs perfectly with myoreps and drop sets since there are no synergists.

name: Leg Extension (Reclined / Extended-Hip, Rectus-Femoris Bias)
rom_notes: The leg-extension tweak from Larsen et al. (2024): recline the backrest so the hip sits near 40 degrees of flexion (more extended) instead of 90, which lengthens the biarticular rectus femoris. Drove ~50-170 percent more rectus-femoris growth (largest at the proximal site) with no loss of vastus-lateralis growth vs the 90-degree seated version. Mitsuya et al. corroborate via MRI activation. Same open-chain knee extension; the only change is hip angle. Conversely, 90-degree (more flexed hip) better suits lifters who want vastus over rectus growth.
regional_bias: rectus femoris (especially proximal/upper) emphasis from the more extended hip
cues: Recline the seat back so your hips open toward 40 degrees rather than sitting bolt upright — this stretches the rectus femoris and grows the upper quad. Lean back, control the lowering, lock out hard.

name: Sissy Squat
rom_notes: Hips stay extended while the knees travel far forward and the torso leans back, driving the knees into deep flexion with the hip open — so the biarticular rectus femoris is stretched at both ends. SBS argues this and the reverse nordic likely beat the leg extension for quad (esp. rectus femoris) growth because they capture the bottom 40-50 degrees of knee-flexion stretch the leg extension misses. Knee-dominant isolation, not a loaded bilateral squat, so it maps to knee extension. Can hold a plate/DB to load (adds grip), or hold a support to assist.
regional_bias: rectus femoris and overall quad at long muscle length; lengthened-bias exercise
cues: Keep hips fully extended (glutes squeezed), let the knees drift forward as you lean the torso back, lower under control into the deep stretch, then extend the knees. Hold a post for balance or a plate on the chest to add load.

name: Reverse Nordic Curl
rom_notes: Kneeling, hips held extended, the lifter leans the whole torso backward so the knees flex under bodyweight while the hip stays open — fully lengthening the rectus femoris. SBS singles it out (alongside the sissy squat) as probably a better rectus-femoris builder than the leg extension because it trains the deeply stretched position the leg extension can't reach. Bodyweight-only loading; scale by how far back you lean or by holding a plate. No grip load.
regional_bias: rectus femoris at extreme length; lengthened-bias quad exercise
cues: Tall kneeling, squeeze the glutes to lock the hips, lean straight back from the knees only, keep the body in one line from knee to head. Lower as far as you control, then pull yourself back up with the quads. Reduce range or hold a support if it's too hard.

name: Bulgarian Split Squat (Dumbbell)
rom_notes: Rear foot elevated, the front leg does almost all the work through a long range; a more upright torso and forward knee travel bias the quad, while a forward lean shifts it toward the glute. Deep front-knee flexion loads the quad at long length. Dumbbells held at the sides load the closed hands directly — grip becomes a real demand as DBs get heavy.
regional_bias: front-leg quad; upright torso = more quad, forward lean = more glute
cues: Rear foot on a bench, most weight on the front foot, drop straight down so the front knee travels forward over the toes for a quad bias. Keep the torso fairly upright. Heavy DBs will tax your grip — use straps if grip fails before the quads.

name: Bulgarian Split Squat (Barbell)
rom_notes: Same unilateral knee-dominant pattern as the DB version but with the bar on the back, removing the grip ceiling so the front leg can be loaded heavier and pushed deeper. Bar supported on traps — low grip demand. More balance and core demand than the DB version.
regional_bias: front-leg quad with deep-ROM long-length loading
cues: Bar on the traps, rear foot elevated, sink straight down on the front leg with the knee tracking forward. Brace the core to stay balanced. Lets you go heavier than dumbbells once grip would otherwise limit you.

name: Walking Lunge (Dumbbell)
rom_notes: Stepping forward into a deep lunge alternating legs; a shorter step with vertical shin and forward knee travel biases the quad, a longer step biases the glute. Long ROM per leg and a stretch on the trailing/front quad. Dumbbells hang from the hands the whole set, so grip and forearms are loaded continuously.
regional_bias: front-leg quad on short steps; more glute/hamstring on long steps
cues: Take a moderate step, drop the back knee toward the floor, keep the front shin fairly vertical for a quad bias. Push off the front foot to step through. The hanging dumbbells load your grip the whole way.

name: Walking Lunge (Barbell)
rom_notes: Same alternating-lunge pattern with the bar on the back, removing the grip limit so the legs can be loaded heavier. Higher balance and axial/core demand than the DB version. Bar supported on traps — low grip demand.
regional_bias: front-leg quad; step length shifts quad vs glute share
cues: Bar on the traps, brace hard, step into a controlled lunge with the front shin vertical for quad emphasis, drive through to the next step. Stay tall and balanced.

name: Dumbbell Step-Up
rom_notes: Driving up onto a box with one leg; box height sets ROM — a higher box increases knee flexion and quad stretch on the working leg (also raises glute demand). Minimize pushing off the trailing foot to keep tension on the working quad. Dumbbells held at the sides load the closed hands throughout. A suitcase (single-DB, one-side) loading adds an anti-lateral-flexion core demand and concentrates grip on one hand.
regional_bias: working-leg quad; higher box adds glute
cues: Plant the whole foot on the box, drive up through the heel and midfoot of the top leg without pushing off the bottom foot, lower under control. Higher box = more quad stretch. The dumbbells tax your grip the whole set.

name: Goblet Squat
rom_notes: Front-loaded bilateral squat holding a single DB/KB at the chest; the counterweight lets most lifters stay upright and reach a deep, quad-biased bottom. Load is capped by what you can hold at the chest, so it's an accessory/entry squat rather than a heavy anchor. Holding the bell at the chest is a supported grip-load, not a hanging load.
regional_bias: quad-biased via upright torso and deep ROM
cues: Cup the dumbbell or kettlebell against your chest, elbows in, sit straight down between your feet to a deep bottom, keep the chest tall. Drive up. The counterweight helps you stay upright for a strong quad stretch.

name: Pendulum Squat
rom_notes: Back-supported arcing sled (like a hack squat but on a pendulum path) that keeps even resistance through a deep range and loads the bottom stretch hard with minimal lower-back/axial fatigue. Lets you chase very deep knee flexion safely; behaves like the hack squat/leg press family for loading. Pads support the load — no grip demand.
regional_bias: vastii-dominant quad work at long length
cues: Shoulders and back into the pads, feet lower on the platform for max knee travel, descend deep into the stretch, control the bottom, drive up. Great for loading the deep position without taxing the spine.

name: Standing Calf Raise (Machine)
rom_notes: Knee held straight so the gastrocnemius is at length and does the work. Drop heel below the platform into a deep dorsiflexion stretch and hold the painful bottom stretch 1-3 s, then pulse up; the lengthened position is the primary growth driver, so prioritize stretch over peak-contraction hold.
regional_bias: gastrocnemius (knee-straight bias)
cues: Knee dead straight. Sink the heels as low as ankle mobility allows and feel the calf stretch burn; pause, then rise to a hard contraction. Shoulder yoke is axially loaded so brace the spine. Calves recover fast between sets — myoreps/short rests work well.

name: Smith Machine Standing Calf Raise
rom_notes: Stand on a block under the Smith bar, knees locked straight (gastroc bias). Deep dorsiflexion stretch at the bottom with a 1-2 s painful pause. Source flags this as a heavier, more systemically fatiguing axial anchor used early in a block.
regional_bias: gastrocnemius (knee-straight bias)
cues: Bar on traps/upper back, knees locked. Heaviest of the calf anchors — source warns axially-loaded calves in the 5-10 range carry heavy axial fatigue, so weigh the tradeoff. Block under the toes to enable a deep stretch.

name: Barbell Standing Calf Raise
rom_notes: Free barbell on the back, knees straight, toes on a block for a deep dorsiflexion stretch. Balance-limited so ROM at the bottom is often cut short vs a machine; hold the bottom stretch as tolerated.
regional_bias: gastrocnemius (knee-straight bias)
cues: Free-bar version of the standing raise; balance and bar stability cap the load and stretch depth. Use a block under the toes, keep knees locked, control the descent.

name: Single-Leg Standing Calf Raise (Dumbbell)
rom_notes: One leg on a block, free hand holds a wall/rack for balance, other hand holds a dumbbell that hangs from the closed hand. Knee straight (gastroc). Deep dorsiflexion stretch with a 1-2 s pause. Per source, a DB heavy enough to cap a 5-10 set turns this into more of a grip exercise than a calf exercise — keep it light/higher-rep.
regional_bias: gastrocnemius (knee-straight bias)
cues: Load hangs from the hand so grip, not calf, becomes limiting if you go too heavy — favor higher reps. Brace with the free hand, sink into a deep stretch, pause, then drive to the top.

name: Stair / Step Calf Raise (Bodyweight)
rom_notes: Forefoot on a stair edge, knees straight, heels drop well below the step for a maximal dorsiflexion stretch — one of the deepest ROMs available for calves. Hold the painful bottom 1-3 s. Often done single-leg to add load without external weight.
regional_bias: gastrocnemius (knee-straight bias)
