cues: Low-fatigue movement the source recommends adding later in a block / for higher frequency. Deep heel drop, long stretch pause. Go single-leg or hold a light DB once bodyweight gets easy — but watch grip if loading.

name: Dumbbell Stair Calf Raise
rom_notes: Stair calf raise with a dumbbell hanging from the working-side hand, other hand braced. Forefoot on the step, knee straight, heels drop deep for a big dorsiflexion stretch with a 1-2 s pause. Source explicitly: a DB big enough to hit 5-10 reps makes this more of a grip exercise than a calf exercise, so keep reps high.
regional_bias: gastrocnemius (knee-straight bias)
cues: DB hangs in the closed hand — grip caps the load. Per source, don't chase the 5-10 range here or you'll fail on grip first. Deep heel drop on the step, hold the stretch, single-leg for extra calf load.

name: Leg Press Calf Raise
rom_notes: Feet low on the leg-press platform, push the sled with the balls of the feet, knees kept near-straight (slight, fixed knee bend) so the gastroc is the prime mover. Let the platform push the toes back into a deep dorsiflexion stretch and pause; one of the best loadable calf movements with no spinal load.
regional_bias: gastrocnemius (knee near-straight)
cues: No spine load, so you can load heavy and chase deep stretch safely. Keep the safeties engaged. Knees fixed/near-straight for gastroc bias; sink the toes back for the stretch and pause hard at the bottom.

name: Seated Calf Raise (Machine)
rom_notes: Knees bent ~90deg under the thigh pad, which slackens the gastrocnemius and shifts the work to the soleus. Forefoot on the platform, drop the heels for a deep dorsiflexion stretch and hold 1-2 s. Hip-loaded (thigh pad), no spinal compression.
regional_bias: soleus (knee-bent bias)
cues: Knee-bent position takes the gastroc out and isolates the soleus — pair with a standing (gastroc) movement to cover both. Deep heel drop, stretch pause; soleus is endurance-biased so it loves the 15-30 range.

name: Seated Calf Raise (Dumbbell on Knees)
rom_notes: Seated, knees bent ~90deg (soleus bias), a dumbbell or plate rested on the lower thighs just above the knees, forefeet on a block. Drive the heels up; let them drop for a deep dorsiflexion stretch and pause. Load rests on the thighs so the hand only steadies it — grip is supported, not weight-bearing.
regional_bias: soleus (knee-bent bias)
cues: Free-weight stand-in for the seated calf machine. Weight balances on the thighs (hands just stabilize, so no real grip tax). Knees bent for soleus, block under the toes, sink into the stretch and pause.

name: Smith Machine Seated Calf Raise
rom_notes: Seated on a bench under the Smith bar with the bar across the lower thighs and forefeet on a block; knees bent ~90deg for soleus emphasis. Bar guides the path so you can load heavy. Deep dorsiflexion stretch with a bottom pause; toes on a block enable full ROM.
regional_bias: soleus (knee-bent bias)
cues: Bar rides on the lower thighs (knees bent for soleus); hands only steer the bar. Block under the toes, deep heel drop, pause in the stretch. Heavier and more stable than the DB-on-knee version.

name: Donkey Calf Raise
rom_notes: Hips hinged forward ~90deg with the load (pad or partner) over the hips/lower back, knees straight, forefeet on a block. The bent-hip position is classically said to lengthen the gastroc; deep dorsiflexion stretch at the bottom with a 1-3 s pause. Hip-loaded, so no compression of the cervical/thoracic spine.
regional_bias: gastrocnemius (knee-straight, hinged-hip stretch)
cues: Hinge at the hips with a flat back, knees locked straight. Load sits on the hips not the shoulders — a good hip-loaded alternative when shoulder-loaded standing raises bother you. Deep heel drop, pause in the stretch.

name: Hack Squat Calf Raise
rom_notes: Stand in a hack-squat machine facing in or out with shoulders under the pads, knees straight, forefeet on the platform edge. Sled guides the path so you can load and stretch safely. Deep dorsiflexion stretch with a bottom pause; a shoulder-loaded standing-raise variant.
regional_bias: gastrocnemius (knee-straight bias)
cues: Uses the hack sled as a guided standing calf raise — stable and easy to load heavy. Knees straight for gastroc, forefoot on the platform edge, sink into the stretch and pause.

name: Single-Leg Bodyweight Calf Raise
rom_notes: One leg, forefoot on a block or floor, knee straight, free hand braced for balance. Heel drops into a deep dorsiflexion stretch (full ROM if on a block) with a 1-3 s pause. Bodyweight on one leg supplies the load — low fatigue, easy to do frequently.
regional_bias: gastrocnemius (knee-straight bias)
cues: Knee locked, single leg doubles the load vs two-leg bodyweight. Use a block for full stretch ROM; brace the free hand for balance only. Great low-fatigue option to bump calf frequency.

name: Seated Leg-Press Calf Raise (Bent Knee)
rom_notes: On a seated/horizontal leg press with the knees left bent (not extended) and forefeet low on the platform, so the gastroc is slackened and the soleus drives plantarflexion. Push the sled with the balls of the feet; let the toes drift back into a deep dorsiflexion stretch and pause. No spinal load.
regional_bias: soleus (knee-bent bias)
cues: Same press but knees stay bent to bias the soleus — a loadable, spine-free alternative to the seated calf machine. Forefoot low, deep stretch, pause at the bottom.

name: Tibialis Raise (Dorsiflexion)
rom_notes: Heels on the floor or a block, toes free; pull the forefoot up toward the shin (dorsiflexion) against bodyweight, a hooked plate, or a band, then lower under control into plantarflexion stretch. The antagonist to the calf raise — included for balanced lower-leg development and shin/ankle health.
regional_bias: tibialis anterior (shin, calf antagonist)
cues: Trains the shin muscle that opposes the calves — balances lower-leg development and shin splints. Heels planted, lift the toes hard toward the shin, control the way down. Bodyweight, a hooked plate, or an anchored band all work.

name: Standing Calf Raise — Bottom Lengthened Partials
rom_notes: Standing calf raise (knees straight) performed through only the bottom 1/3 to 1/2 of the range — the lengthened/stretched portion — keeping the gastroc loaded at its longest length. Used as a full set or as a stretch-partial burnout after a full-ROM set. Source: loading the muscle at its longest lengths is an extra growth boost.
regional_bias: gastrocnemius, lengthened/stretched range
cues: Stay in the bottom, stretched portion — never come all the way to the top. Loads the calf where it grows best. Run as a dedicated set or tack onto the end of a full-ROM set as a lengthened-partial finisher.

name: Barbell Wrist Curl (Forearms-Over-Bench)
rom_notes: Forearms resting on bench/thighs, hands off the edge. Let the wrist roll into full extension at the bottom (palm bends back), then flex hard at the top. RP warns the wrist flexors hit active insufficiency before joint ROM ends in this propped position, so the very top is low-tension; the deep eccentric stretch is where the growth stimulus lives.
regional_bias: wrist flexors (anterior forearm flexor group)
cues: Pin forearms down so only the wrists move. Roll the bar to the fingertips and let the palm bend fully back, then crunch the fist closed as you curl up. Don't cut the bottom ROM to chase PRs. Myoreps suit this well since forearms recover fast between sets.

name: Dumbbell Wrist Curl
rom_notes: Forearm propped on bench/thigh, one DB. Same active-insufficiency caveat as the barbell version near the top; at the very bottom (hand hanging down) the DB's gravity provides little resistance, so the most-loaded portion is the mid-range eccentric. Single-arm allows light loads and home use.
regional_bias: wrist flexors (anterior forearm flexor group)
cues: Brace the forearm flat. Let the DB roll to the fingertips, bend the palm back, then flex up and squeeze the fist. RP notes single-arm DB wrist curls for sets of 5-10 can bother some wrists; reserve the heaviest work for the standing barbell variant if so.

name: Behind-the-Back Standing Barbell Wrist Curl
rom_notes: Standing, bar held behind the glutes against the body. The wrist can roll into deep extension with the bar clearing the body, and the load line stays more constant through the curl than the bench version. RP treats this as a high-stress fixed staple for the heavier 5-10 / 10-20 ranges.
regional_bias: wrist flexors (anterior forearm flexor group)
cues: Stand tall, bar resting behind the thighs. Roll the bar down the fingers, then curl up flexing the wrists. Your traps work to hold the bar while standing, so let them recover between sets too (RP's 4-factor rest check).

name: Cable Wrist Curl
rom_notes: The Demystified doc's preferred wrist-flexor option: stand back-to-cable, working arm down at the side, attachment set low so the cable pulls the hand backward and slightly down. Constant cable tension keeps load on the muscle through the whole ROM, including the lengthened position where a DB/BB would be slack. Lighter, low-fatigue, lengthened-biased.
regional_bias: wrist flexors, lengthened bias
cues: Back to the stack, arm pinned at your side, elbow flexed for comfort. Let the cable pull the wrist into extension, then curl through. Tension never drops, so cheating ROM is hard. Great for the light 20-30 rep work RP says forearms respond to.

name: Finger-Rolling Wrist Curl (Dynamic Finger Curl)
rom_notes: SBS's preferred finger-flexor builder: let the bar roll down to the fingertips and the metacarpophalangeal joints extend on the eccentric, then re-curl the fingers and flex the wrist. Trains both wrist flexion AND dynamic finger flexion at long lengths, plus the intrinsic hand muscles. Finish with pure finger-curl reps as a mechanical drop set once wrist-curl reps fail.
regional_bias: finger flexors (flexor digitorum) at long lengths
cues: Let the implement roll to the fingertips and the fingers open, but not so far it slides out. Curl the fingers back closed, then flex the wrist. Use lighter load than a standard wrist curl (longer lever as it rolls out). End the set with pure finger curls. SBS's top hypertrophy pick for the finger flexors.

name: Barbell Reverse Wrist Curl (Wrist Extension)
rom_notes: Pronated grip, forearms parallel to ground over bench/thighs. No active-insufficiency problem here, so it's easy to load the extensors properly through full ROM. SBS notes wrist-extension training raised grip force ~19% in 8 weeks by helping the wrist sit at its optimal extended angle for the finger flexors. Strap up if grip fades — grip isn't the target.
regional_bias: wrist extensors (forearm extensor group)
cues: Forearms flat, knuckles down. Lower into wrist flexion, then extend the wrist to lift the back of the hand. Lighter than wrist flexion. RP recommends 5-10 sets/week of extension vs 3-6 for flexion since extensors tolerate more.

name: Dumbbell Reverse Wrist Curl
rom_notes: Single-arm pronated wrist extension, forearm propped. Same favorable loading as the barbell version with unilateral control and light-load convenience. Wrist extension can be trained any day with little interference to other work.
regional_bias: wrist extensors (forearm extensor group)
cues: Forearm pinned flat, knuckles facing down. Extend the wrist to raise the DB, lower under control. One arm at a time lets you focus and use very light loads.

name: Cable Reverse Wrist Curl
rom_notes: Pronated cable wrist extension giving constant tension through the full ROM including the stretched position, unlike free weights where the bottom can go slack. Low joint stress, easy to load lightly for high-rep work.
regional_bias: wrist extensors, constant-tension
cues: Pronated grip on a low pulley handle, forearm supported. Extend the wrist against the cable, control the return. Constant tension makes ROM-cheating hard; good for high-rep extensor work.

name: Barbell Reverse Curl
rom_notes: Pronated-grip elbow flexion. The pronated forearm position mechanically optimizes the brachioradialis line of pull relative to the biceps/brachialis, making it a prime brachioradialis builder. Also loads the wrist extensors isometrically to hold the pronated wrist. EZ-bar reduces wrist strain vs straight bar.
regional_bias: brachioradialis (radial forearm)
cues: Overhand (pronated) grip, keep the wrist neutral/slightly extended — don't let it flex. Curl with the elbows pinned. A single weekly session of reverse or hammer curls can bring the brachioradialis into MEV-MRV per RP.

name: Dumbbell Hammer Curl
rom_notes: Neutral (thumbs-up) grip elbow flexion. The neutral-to-pronated forearm orientation primes the brachioradialis while the brachialis and biceps assist. The Demystified doc calls this and rope cable curls fine brachioradialis isolation options. Can be done alternating or simultaneously, seated or standing.
regional_bias: brachioradialis + brachialis
cues: Palms facing each other throughout. Keep the forearm neutral; don't rotate. Drive with the elbow, control the lowering. Pairs well at the end of back day where the brachioradialis is already warm from pulling.

name: Rope Cable Hammer Curl
rom_notes: Neutral-grip elbow flexion off a low pulley with a rope, giving constant tension through the curl. Demystified doc names rope cable curls as a fine brachioradialis isolation option. Lower joint stress than free-weight hammer curls; constant tension keeps the top loaded.
regional_bias: brachioradialis + brachialis, constant-tension
cues: Neutral grip on the rope ends, elbows pinned to the sides. Curl up keeping the wrists neutral, spread the rope slightly at the top. Constant cable tension makes it easy to keep strict form.

name: Wrist Roller
rom_notes: A weight on a cord wound onto a bar by alternately twisting the hands. As one wrist flexes the other extends, so it trains flexion and extension in one tool. Demystified doc calls it a fine option assuming proper overload is logistically possible; demands diligent full, purposeful ROM. Held out in front, so it's also a sustained grip/anterior-delt isometric.
regional_bias: wrist flexors and extensors together
cues: Wind the weight all the way up and lower it under control — don't just flick the wrists. Hold the bar out front. The closed fists grip the bar the whole set, so expect a heavy forearm and grip burn.

name: Hand Gripper Crush
rom_notes: Torsion-spring gripper closed by crushing the fingers. SBS notes it trains dynamic finger flexion at longer lengths than most support-grip work, holding the wrist extended while loading the intrinsic hand muscles. RP: work 10-30 reps, open the gripper as wide as you can and hold a 1-second full-close. Portable, minimal systemic fatigue, train anywhere.
regional_bias: finger flexors (crush-grip group)
cues: Open the hand as wide as the gripper allows for a long-length stretch, crush to a full close, hold ~1 second. Keep the wrist slightly extended. Humbling but loads the finger flexors dynamically where support grip can't.

name: Plate Pinch Hold
rom_notes: Pinch one or more smooth-side-out plates (or a pinch block) between thumb and fingers; isometric pinch hold. SBS: trains finger flexors at long lengths, imparts low axial loading and low skin stress vs knurled support grip. Open-hand thumb-vs-fingers emphasis. Hand/finger length is a big performance limiter. Can be a static hold or loaded into a unilateral pinch carry.
regional_bias: finger flexors + thumb adductors at long lengths
cues: Smooth faces out, pinch with thumb opposing the fingers — distal pads on the plate is hardest. Chalk and dry hands matter since it's pure friction. Pick a load that nears grip failure in 20-40s. Thin iron plates: stack several.

name: Dead Hang (Bar Hang)
rom_notes: Bodyweight hang from a pull-up bar to grip failure. SBS values it as a support-grip builder that simultaneously decompresses the spine (no axial compression) and trains overhead shoulder mobility. Progress to unilateral hangs or added weight. Isometric, so good for grip strength/endurance more than hypertrophy.
regional_bias: support-grip finger flexors
cues: Full double-overhand grip, hang passively or with active shoulders. Pick a load (bodyweight, +weight, or single-arm) that nears grip failure in 20-40s. For one-arm hangs, lightly steady yourself against a rack to stop spinning without unloading the working side.

name: Farmer's Carry
rom_notes: Walking while holding heavy loads in both hands; bilateral support grip with neutral wrist and flexed fingers held to failure. Trains finger flexors at moderately short lengths plus heavy trap/erector/core stabilization. Load hangs from the closed hands the entire walk.
regional_bias: support-grip finger flexors; traps
tempo: steady brisk walk to grip failure
cues: Stand tall, ribs down, crush the handles. Walk briskly with short steps. Pick a load that taxes grip near failure in ~20-40s. Heavier kettlebell/thick handles increase the grip demand. Don't strap if grip is the target.

name: Suitcase / Barbell Rack-Pull Hold
rom_notes: Static barbell hold from above-the-knee rack/block height to develop deadlift-specific support grip at the exact finger angles used when pulling. SBS programs it as 20-40s holds for support grip strength. Adding fat grips lets lighter loads provide the same grip stimulus, sparing the spine from heavy compressive loading.
regional_bias: deadlift-specific support-grip finger flexors
cues: Set the bar at/above the knee, take your deadlift grip, lift to lockout and hold until grip nears failure (~20-40s). Use a double-overhand grip to challenge grip (not mixed). Add fat grips to drop the load and spare the lower back. Pre-exhaust option: wrist curls into a static hold (RP) — it hurts but works.

name: Fat-Grip (Thick-Bar) Dumbbell Row
rom_notes: A strict dumbbell row with a fat-grip attachment (or axle/thick handle) added so grip becomes a meaningful stimulus by set's end without sacrificing back stimulus. SBS's headline use of fat grips: take a support-grip lift you already do where grip isn't the limiter and make it train grip too; the thicker handle also loads finger flexors at longer lengths. Finish with a static hold to push grip to failure.
regional_bias: lats with added finger-flexor support-grip stimulus
cues: Use strict technique (controlled eccentric, paused top/bottom) so the fat grip doesn't cut your row weight. Pick a fat-grip size that lets you match your normal reps; add a static hold after the last rep to drive grip to failure. Don't use it on cheat-rows where it tanks the load.

name: Weighted Forearm Pronation / Supination
rom_notes: Rotate the forearm from palm-down (pronation, pronator teres) to palm-up (supination, supinator) against an asymmetrically loaded handle/DB, forearm supported. SBS programs it for forearm mass and wrist-rotation strength (e.g., arm wrestling). Niche accessory; the supinator/pronator are small with limited size potential but trainable for specific demands.
regional_bias: pronator teres / supinator (forearm rotators)
cues: Forearm braced on a bench, hold an offset/asymmetric load. Rotate fully palm-up then palm-down under control. Niche — mainly worth it for arm-wrestling or rotational-strength goals, not general forearm size.

name: Wide-Grip Lat Pulldown
rom_notes: Full ROM from a near-fully-extended overhead stretch to bar at upper chest with elbows driven down to the sides. Thigh pad anchors the body. Avoid leaning back into a row; pull to clavicle, not behind the neck.
regional_bias: upper/outer lats (wide grip emphasizes shoulder adduction; Sperandei found wide pronated grip the highest lat:biceps ratio of the pulldown variants)
cues: Set the thigh pad snug, grip ~150% of biacromial width, depress the shoulder blades to start, drive elbows down and in toward the ribs, squeeze a brief peak at the bottom, control the stretch up to a deep hang. Lat:biceps activation barely changes with grip width, so chase a deep stretch over an extreme width.

name: Close Neutral-Grip Lat Pulldown
rom_notes: Greater achievable ROM than wide grip because the elbows can travel further down past the torso, giving more shoulder extension at the bottom and a longer pull. Neutral V-handle.
regional_bias: lower lats (close/neutral grip allows more shoulder extension, biasing lower lat fibers; neutral grip is wrist-friendly)
cues: Pull the handle to the upper chest, let the elbows pass your sides for a longer shoulder-extension stroke, brief squeeze, full stretch overhead. Neutral grip reduces wrist and elbow stress vs straight bar.

name: Reverse-Grip (Underhand) Lat Pulldown
rom_notes: Supinated shoulder-width grip; elbows track close to the body and pull deep into shoulder extension, giving a long lower-lat stroke. Bar to upper chest/sternum.
regional_bias: lower lats with more biceps involvement (supination slightly raises biceps and lowers the lat:biceps ratio vs wide grip per Sperandei, but lat activation itself is statistically unchanged)
cues: Palms facing you at shoulder width, drive the elbows down and back into your sides, pull to the sternum. Despite gym lore, the supinated grip does not turn this into a biceps exercise; the lat is still the prime mover. Good rotation partner for overhand work across the week.

name: Single-Arm Cable Lat Pulldown
rom_notes: Single D-handle from a high pulley; the free side allows extra ROM at the top stretch (the shoulder can reach higher) and a longer pull at the bottom than a fixed bar. Kneeling or seated.
regional_bias: full lat with extended stretch range; lets each side reach an unrestricted overhead stretch and bottom contraction
cues: Reach tall at the top to maximize lat stretch, pull the elbow down to the hip, resist trunk rotation with the obliques. Train both sides to equal reps. Unilateral loading lets the working lat go through a fuller arc than a barred pulldown.

name: Pull-Up (Pronated/Overhand)
rom_notes: Dead hang at the bottom to chin-over-bar at the top. RP emphasizes full ROM: down to a true dead hang and up until the chin clears the bar; partial mid-range reps are sub-optimal.
regional_bias: upper/outer lats (pronated, wider hand spacing biases shoulder adduction and upper lat fibers)
cues: Start from a full dead hang, depress and retract the shoulder blades, pull the chest toward the bar until the chin clears it, lower under control to a full stretch. Grip endurance is a real limiter on rep count, so train forearms if grip fails before the lats do. Pause at the bottom to standardize tracking.

name: Weighted Pull-Up
rom_notes: Same dead-hang-to-chin-over-bar ROM as a bodyweight pull-up but loaded with a dip belt, plate, or dumbbell between the feet. Best kept in lower reps because the whole point is greater absolute force.
regional_bias: upper/outer lats; a primary heavy vertical-pull anchor (RP pairs weighted pull-ups with barbell rows as the heavy back staples)
cues: Add load via belt or plate between the ankles, keep reps in the 5-10 range to impose high absolute force, full dead hang to chin over bar each rep. Pause at the bottom for safe, trackable reps. Heavy grip demand; straps are an option if grip fails first, though they do not increase lat work.

name: Chin-Up (Supinated/Underhand)
rom_notes: Supinated shoulder-width grip; dead hang to chin over bar. Elbows drive forward then down, producing more shoulder extension and a deep lower-lat/biceps stretch at the bottom.
regional_bias: lower lats plus heavy biceps (close supinated grip = shoulder extension; chin-ups are a notable biceps stimulus, comparable to curls)
cues: Palms toward you at shoulder width, dead hang to start, drive the elbows down and slightly forward, chin over the bar. Rotate with overhand pull-ups across the week so different motor-unit pools share the load. Doubles as effective direct biceps work.

name: Neutral-Grip Pull-Up
rom_notes: Palms-facing parallel handles; dead hang to chin/upper-chest over the bar. Wrist-neutral path is the most shoulder- and elbow-friendly pull-up variant.
regional_bias: lower/mid lats with strong brachialis-brachioradialis involvement; joint-friendly intermediate between pull-up and chin-up
cues: Grip the parallel handles, dead hang, pull until the bar is at upper-chest height, control the descent. The neutral wrist spares the elbows and shoulders, making it a good substitute when pronated or supinated grips aggravate joints.

name: Assisted Pull-Up (Machine)
rom_notes: Knee or foot platform applies counterweight to offset bodyweight; full dead-hang-to-chin-over-bar ROM at a scaled load. Lets sub-bodyweight lifters train the pull-up pattern through full range.
regional_bias: same as the chosen grip (pronated upper-lat / neutral / supinated lower-lat); regression tool to build to a free pull-up
cues: Set the counterweight so the last reps are near failure, kneel or stand on the pad, pull through the full range to the bar. Reduce assistance over weeks to progress toward unassisted pull-ups. Still loads the grip via the hanging hand.

name: Band-Assisted Pull-Up
rom_notes: Loop band under the foot or knee gives the most assistance at the bottom stretch (where the band is most stretched) and least at the top. Full dead hang to chin over bar. Note the band under-assists the hard top portion.
regional_bias: same as chosen grip; band offloads the bottom stretch most, so it eases the hardest portion least near the top contraction
cues: Hook the band on the bar and place a foot or knee in the loop, dead hang, pull to chin over bar. Use a lighter band as you get stronger. Because band tension is highest at the bottom, it assists the stretch most and the contraction least.

name: Plate-Loaded Iso-Lateral Pulldown Machine
rom_notes: Chest pad supports the torso; independent arms (iso-lateral) allow each side a full overhead-stretch-to-contracted ROM. Fixed path means no balance demand, ideal for high-rep mind-muscle work.
regional_bias: lats with a chest-supported, stable line of pull; iso-lateral arms let each lat work through its own full arc and fix imbalances
cues: Brace the chest into the pad, reach up for a full stretch, drive the handles down to your sides, brief squeeze. The fixed path makes this excellent for higher-rep giant sets and mind-muscle focus where free pull-ups would tax the grip and support muscles too early.

name: Straight-Arm Cable Pulldown
rom_notes: Pure shoulder extension with the elbows nearly locked; arc the straight (or near-straight) arms from overhead down to the thighs. Isolates the lat without elbow flexion, so the biceps and grip are largely removed as limiters.
regional_bias: lats through shoulder extension with minimal arm involvement; the long head of the triceps assists as a shoulder extensor (straight-arm pulldowns can drive high long-head triceps activity)
cues: Stand back from a high pulley, hinge slightly, keep arms straight, pull the bar in an arc to your thighs by extending the shoulders, squeeze the lats. Has essentially no synergist limiter, so it suits myoreps and pre-exhaust supersets before pulldowns. A great mind-muscle tool for lifters who struggle to feel their lats.

name: Lat Prayer (Cable Straight-Arm Pullover with Body English)
rom_notes: Straight-arm cable pullover with deliberate torso movement: lean forward to a horizontal torso for a deep lat stretch at the top, lean back to vertical for peak contraction at the bottom. Arms stay straight, stopping short of full 180-degree overhead (aim 120-170-degree) to keep tension on the lats not connective tissue.
regional_bias: lats through their entire length, with the greatest resistance in full contraction; matches the lat's strength curve better than rows or pulldowns and trains the long lengthened position rows omit
cues: Kneel or stand at a high pulley with a rope or V/W handle, lean into the stretch up top, pull straight arms into your lap while leaning back, elbows finishing in line with the torso. Move the torso to match resistance to strength: stretch forward on the ascent, contract back on the descent. Fail in the bottom contracted position to protect the shoulder. Do not let arms bend (that turns it into a pulldown-plus-pushdown) and do not let the weight drag you past the lats' active ROM overhead.

name: Dumbbell Pullover
rom_notes: Lying across or along a bench, lower a single dumbbell in an arc behind the head for a deep lat/pec stretch, then pull it back over the chest via shoulder extension. Loads the deep stretch heavily; resistance falls off as the arms come vertical. Hard to load heavily and somewhat shoulder-stressful.
regional_bias: lats and lower pec at the stretched position; trains the lengthened position rows skip but loses tension as the arms reach vertical
cues: Hold one dumbbell cupped in both hands over the chest, lower it behind the head with slightly bent arms for a deep stretch, pull back over the chest. The closed hands crush-grip and bear the hanging dumbbell, so grip and elbow load are real. Stop before the shoulder is forced past comfortable end-range to avoid impingement.

name: Behind-the-Neck Lat Pulldown
rom_notes: Wide pronated grip pulled behind the head to the base of the neck; requires forced external rotation and forward head posture. Shorter, more constrained ROM than a front pulldown and higher shoulder stress.
regional_bias: upper lats and traps; produces no more lat activation than front pulldowns while adding shoulder/neck risk, so it is a lower-priority variant
cues: Use only if you have ample shoulder external rotation and mobility; keep the load light, pull to the neck base without crunching the neck forward. Generally pull to the front instead, since the behind-neck path adds joint stress without a hypertrophy advantage. Included for completeness as a known variant.

name: Sternum (Gironda) Chin-Up
rom_notes: Exaggerated lean-back pull-up where the torso arches and the lower sternum/upper abdomen is pulled toward the bar, finishing in deep shoulder extension. Larger contracted-range arc than a standard pull-up; demanding on the lower lats.
regional_bias: lower lats via deep shoulder extension in the contracted position; a contraction-emphasis bodyweight vertical pull
cues: Lean the torso back and arch as you pull, aiming to touch the lower sternum to the bar with elbows driving down and back into full shoulder extension. Strong contraction emphasis; control the eccentric. Advanced variant, keep loads bodyweight until the pattern is grooved.

name: Kneeling Banded Lat Pulldown
rom_notes: Band anchored overhead; kneel and pull down to the chest (bent-arm) or to the thighs (straight-arm). Resistance rises through the pull (ascending band tension), peaking at the contracted bottom and easing at the overhead stretch.
regional_bias: lats with peak tension at the contracted bottom (band tension is highest there); a travel/home substitute for the cable pulldown
cues: Anchor the band to a high point, kneel under it, depress the shoulder blades and pull the elbows down to the sides. Band tension ascends through the rep so it loads the contraction hardest and the stretch least, the inverse of a pull-up's profile. Useful when no cable or machine is available.

name: Commando (Mixed-Grip) Pull-Up
rom_notes: Straddle the bar with one hand in front of the other (mixed grip), pulling the head alternately to each side of the bar. Asymmetric ROM and a strong anti-rotation core demand alongside the vertical pull.
regional_bias: lats with heavy oblique/core anti-rotation; the alternating-side path biases the lat on the side the head rises toward
cues: Grip the bar in line with your body, one hand ahead of the other, pull up bringing your head to one side then alternate sides each rep. Brace hard to resist rotation. A novelty/core-integrated vertical pull; alternate which hand leads to balance the obliques.

name: Barbell Hip Thrust
rom_notes: Shoulder blades on bench, full hip extension to lockout with posterior pelvic tilt; glute peak-contracted at top (terminal hip extension), unlike squat the torque curve peaks where the glute does most work. Optional 1-2s top hold.
regional_bias: upper gluteus maximus (highest EMG of the loaded bilateral lifts; ~82% MVIC traditional, upper GM ~87% vs lower GM ~70%)
cues: Tuck chin, ribs down, push through heels, drive hips straight up and squeeze glutes hard at lockout; avoid hyperextending the low back. Bar pad over hip crease.

name: American Hip Thrust
rom_notes: Variant biasing the upper GM via increased anterior pelvic motion/different bench contact; full hip extension to lockout.
regional_bias: upper gluteus maximus (American style upper GM ~90% vs lower GM ~57% MVIC)
cues: Keep posterior pelvic tilt, drive through heels; emphasize a full upper-glute squeeze at terminal extension.

name: Machine Hip Thrust
rom_notes: Padded back support and lap belt/pad; same horizontal hip-extension torque profile as the barbell version but more stable and lower setup/skill cost. Full lockout with top squeeze.
regional_bias: upper gluteus maximus; very high SFR due to spinal/setup offload vs barbell
cues: Set seat so hip crease aligns with pad, drive through heels to full lockout, hold the squeeze, control the eccentric to a deep hip-flexed stretch.

name: Smith Machine Hip Thrust
rom_notes: Fixed bar path removes balance demand; same terminal hip-extension peak torque as the barbell hip thrust. Full lockout, optional top hold.
regional_bias: upper gluteus maximus
cues: Position shoulders on bench, bar over hip crease with pad, push through heels to lockout, squeeze glutes; let the fixed path let you focus purely on hip drive.

name: Single-Leg Hip Thrust
rom_notes: One working leg drives the hip to full extension; the unilateral demand adds frontal-plane stabilization so the gluteus medius works to keep the pelvis level. Optional dumbbell on the hip for load.
regional_bias: gluteus maximus + added gluteus medius (pelvic-leveling) demand
cues: Keep hips square, push through the working heel to lockout, squeeze; don't let the pelvis drop on the free side.

name: Barbell Glute Bridge
rom_notes: Back flat on floor (shorter ROM than hip thrust); a shorter-lever bridge with knees more flexed reduces hamstring contribution via active insufficiency, making GMax the primary agonist. Full hip extension with top squeeze.
regional_bias: gluteus maximus (short-lever knee angle reduces hamstring share)
cues: Heels close to glutes (short lever) to deload hamstrings, drive hips up, squeeze hard at top; focus on the mind-muscle connection rather than just repping out.

name: Frog Pump
rom_notes: Soles of feet together, knees splayed out (hip external rotation/abduction), bridge the hips up. The externally rotated/abducted position biases the GMax and shortens hamstring leverage. Short-ROM high-rep pump movement.
regional_bias: gluteus maximus (abducted/externally-rotated setup increases GM share, reduces hamstring)
cues: Soles together, push knees out, drive hips up by squeezing glutes; chase the burn/pump, not max load.

name: Cable Glute Kickback
rom_notes: Ankle cuff on a low pulley; extend the hip behind the body against the cable's near-constant tension. Pure single-joint hip extension with a strong shortened-position contraction and a good stretch at the front.
regional_bias: gluteus maximus (lower fibers, terminal hip extension); minimal systemic/synergist fatigue so very high SFR with short rest
cues: Hinge slightly forward, brace, kick the leg straight back and squeeze the glute at end range; keep the low back still and let the hip do the work. Short rests (<45s) are fine.

name: Machine Glute Kickback
rom_notes: Foot/shin on a lever pad, torso supported; drive the hip into extension against the machine. Stable, low-skill isolation with a controlled stretch and a strong shortened contraction.
regional_bias: gluteus maximus; very high SFR (single leg, low body-support and CNS cost, short rest)
cues: Brace against the support pad, push the working leg back to full hip extension, squeeze; control the return into a hip-flexed stretch.

name: Seated Hip Abduction Machine
rom_notes: Seated, pads on outer thighs; press the knees apart (hip abduction). Leaning the torso forward shifts emphasis toward the upper GMax fibers (which also abduct); upright biases gluteus medius/minimus. Full ROM out to a strong abducted squeeze.
regional_bias: gluteus medius/minimus and upper (superior) gluteus maximus fibers; lean forward to bias upper GMax
cues: Drive the knees apart through full range, squeeze at the outer position, control back in; lean the torso forward to shift toward upper glute fibers.

name: Cable Standing Hip Abduction
rom_notes: Ankle cuff on a low pulley, stand side-on; raise the working leg out to the side against constant cable tension. Pure frontal-plane abduction with smooth resistance through ROM.
regional_bias: gluteus medius/minimus (frontal-plane abductors)
cues: Stand tall, brace the trunk, lift the leg out and slightly back, squeeze; avoid hiking the hip or leaning the torso to cheat the rep.

name: Banded Hip Abduction
rom_notes: Loop band around knees/ankles; abduct against band tension (seated press-outs, lateral walks, or standing abductions). A knee band during squats/bridges also raises GMax and gluteus medius activation by adding abduction work.
regional_bias: gluteus medius/minimus and upper gluteus maximus; band tension increases activation but resistance is light/ascending
cues: Keep constant outward tension on the band, drive the knees apart, don't let them collapse in on the return; squeeze the outer glutes each rep.

name: Banded Clamshell
rom_notes: Side-lying, hips/knees flexed, feet together; rotate the top knee open (hip external rotation + abduction) against a knee band. A classic non-weight-bearing gluteal activation drill targeting the posterior/superior gluteus medius.
regional_bias: gluteus medius (posterior fibers) + gluteus maximus external-rotation function; low loadability limits the hypertrophy stimulus
cues: Keep feet stacked together and the pelvis from rolling back, open the knee by squeezing the glute, pause at the top; small slow reps beat momentum.

name: Romanian Deadlift (Glute-Biased)
rom_notes: Hip hinge from standing with soft knees; loads the glute and hamstrings deeply in the stretched (hip-flexed) position. Sit the hips back further and drive to a hard hip-extension lockout to bias the glute share of the hinge; the bar stays close to the legs.
regional_bias: gluteus maximus + hamstrings at long muscle length; stiff-leg/RDL hinge ~40% GMax MVIC, glute share rises with a hard lockout and posterior hip drive
cues: Push the hips back, keep the bar dragging the thighs, feel the glute/hamstring stretch, then snap the hips through to a tall glute-squeezed lockout; neutral spine throughout. Double-overhand grip (straps for top sets if grip limits).

name: Sumo Deficit Deadlift
rom_notes: Wide stance, hips deep, standing on a low plate (deficit) to increase hip flexion and glute stretch at the bottom. A heavy axial compound RP cites as a core glute pull done in the 5-10 range.
regional_bias: gluteus maximus with heavy adductor magnus involvement from the wide stance; the deficit adds bottom-range stretch
cues: Wide stance, hips down and through, spread the floor with the knees, drive to a glute-locked stand; the deficit deepens the stretch so keep a braced neutral spine. Straps optional on top sets.

name: Dumbbell Step-Up
rom_notes: Step one foot onto a box and drive up to a single-leg stand; a high box increases hip flexion (glute stretch) at the bottom. Unilateral weight-bearing means the GMax extends the hip while the gluteus medius levels the pelvis, which is why EMG ranks step-ups the highest of all glute exercises (~125-169% MVIC).
regional_bias: gluteus maximus + gluteus medius (highest GMax EMG of any reviewed exercise; a high box biases the glute)
cues: Use a box high enough to feel the glute stretch, drive through the lead heel without pushing off the trailing foot, stand tall; control the lower. Hold dumbbells at the sides (grip loaded).

name: Lateral Step-Up
rom_notes: Step up sideways (lateral) or across the body (crossover) onto a box. The frontal-plane entry adds large gluteus medius/minimus stabilization demand on top of hip extension; lateral/crossover step-ups rank among the very-highest GMax EMG (~104-114% MVIC).
regional_bias: gluteus maximus with heavy gluteus medius/minimus involvement (frontal-plane stabilization)
cues: Plant the working foot fully on the box, drive up through the heel without bouncing off the floor leg, keep the pelvis level; lower under control. Dumbbells held at sides.

name: Barbell Walking Lunge
rom_notes: Alternating forward strides with a deep lunge; a long stride and deep descent maximize the glute stretch on the lead leg. RP's primary 'lunge category' movement, best run in the 20-30 rep range. Traditional/in-line lunge ~66-67% GMax MVIC (very high).
regional_bias: gluteus maximus (deep lunge stretch) + gluteus medius stabilization
cues: Take a long stride, drop the back knee toward the floor for a deep glute stretch, drive up through the front heel; keep the torso tall and the pelvis stable. Bar on back (low grip demand).

name: Bulgarian Split Squat (Glute-Biased)
rom_notes: Rear foot elevated on a bench; a longer stance and a forward torso lean increase hip flexion and bias the glute over the quad. Deep ROM heavily stretches the lead glute. Split squat ~70% GMax MVIC (very high).
regional_bias: gluteus maximus (lengthened position via forward lean + long stance) with gluteus medius stabilization
cues: Stride out far and hinge the torso slightly forward to bias the glute, descend deep into the lead-hip stretch, drive up through the front heel; keep the pelvis square. Dumbbells held at sides.

name: Reverse Hyperextension
rom_notes: Torso supported face-down on a pad, legs hang and swing up into hip extension against a pendulum/strap load. Trains hip extension with little spinal compression and a strong glute-shortened contraction at the top.
regional_bias: gluteus maximus + hamstrings (terminal hip extension, low spinal load)
cues: Hold the handles, brace the trunk, swing the legs up to hip extension by squeezing the glutes (don't hyperextend the back), control the descent; avoid using momentum.
